Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data Sophie L. Wang Amil Dravid Rulin Shao Kevin Farhat Sewon Min Alexei A. Efros Abstract In this paper, we study how training data creates associations between the tokens at the start of a base model’s response and the reasoning behavior that follows. First, we demonstrate that fixing particular starting token cues makes a base model’s performance competitive with that of its reinforcement learning (RL)-trained counterparts on math and coding. For instance, the cue Ay .

 Ay Okay raises Olmo-3-7B’s MATH-500 pass@1 accuracy from 42% to 78%, while Ay ␣Alright Ay , raises Qwen3-14B’s from 72% to 87%. Second, RL makes these cues more likely, while fixing them recovers much of its performance gain over the base model. Third, we trace the reasoning effects of token cues to the training data. We perform causal data interventions to turn an arbitrary word, such as “chicken”, into an effective reasoning cue, or remove an existing cue’s effect. A similar edit makes the prompt instruction “Think duck duck goose” as effective as “Think step by step” at eliciting reasoning. We also find that the hidden state representations induced by different cues correlate with different document types from the training set. Finally, we extend our study of token cues with a case study in language model safety, finding that different cues elicit distinct refusal and compliance behaviors that correspond to different types of training data. Project Page: sophielwang.com/cues Code: github.com/sophicle/cues Figure 1 : A base model’s first tokens steer reasoning behavior through associations learned from training data. ( Top ) Olmo-3-7B’s next-token probabilities are conditioned on the prompt and preceding tokens. Starting with Ay .
 Ay Answer leads to a short answer , whereas Ay .

 Ay Okay leads to deliberation and reasoning performance comparable to RL ( Sec. 2.2 ). RL increases the probability of the reasoning cue Ay .

 Ay Okay ( Sec. 2.3 ). Replacing “okay” with “chicken” in mid-training data makes Ay .

 Ay Chicken elicit reasoning too ( Sec. 3.1 ). Representational analysis connects these behaviors to training data ( Sec. 3.2 ). ( Bottom ) MATH-500 pass@1 for each opening on the base model, after RL, and after the data edit on the 100B-token mid-training mix. 1 Introduction While studying digestion, Ivan Pavlov noticed that dogs salivated when observing stimuli associated with feeding (e.g., seeing the food bowl), even before food arrived ( Pavlov, 1927 ) . But surprisingly, he could make an arbitrary stimulus (e.g., ringing a bell) elicit the same response through conditioning (repeated association), despite the stimulus playing no role in digestion. In base language models, we similarly find that short token cues can elicit behaviors such as reasoning ( Fig. 1 ). For example, fixing only the first two tokens of a base model’s response can bring its performance close to that of its counterpart post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL). Furthermore, even an arbitrary token can be conditioned to trigger reasoning behavior by replacing an existing cue in the training data. What does it mean, then, for a language model to learn to “reason”? A growing body of work asks what reasoning capabilities base models already possess and what post-training adds. Although base models learn through next-token prediction on general text corpora, behaviors such as reflection and verification have been described as emerging during reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Yet, observing a behavior after post-training does not establish that the ability to produce it was absent beforehand. This leaves open whether RL teaches novel reasoning capabilities or merely exploits capabilities acquired beforehand ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Gan and Isola, 2026 ) . Indeed, base models have been found to exhibit reasoning through techniques like explicit prompting and inference-time search strategies ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Wang and Zhou, 2024 ; Karan and Du, 2026 ) . So, if reasoning may already be present in the base model, how little intervention is needed to elicit it? In this paper, we show that fixing just the first two tokens of a base model’s response can bring its reasoning performance to the level of its RL-trained counterpart ( Sec. 2 ). These token cues can be as simple as Ay .

 Ay Okay for Olmo-3-7B or Ay ␣Alright Ay , for Qwen3-14B. These fixed openings yield substantial gains across the evaluated benchmarks, despite providing neither a demonstration nor an instruction to reason. For example, on MATH-500, the cue raises Olmo-3-7B’s pass@1 accuracy from 42% to 78%, compared with 75% for its RL counterpart. RL itself increases the probability of these cues, with policy changes concentrated at the first few output positions. Moreover, forcing the cue in training rollouts can reach comparable accuracy in fewer RL updates. To investigate why these token cues elicit reasoning in base models, we turn to the training data ( Sec. 3 ). Analogous to Pavlov’s conditioning experiments, we test whether particular tokens trigger reasoning behavior because of associations learned during training. We retrain Olmo-3-7B from an intermediate checkpoint on edited data and extend the experiments to SmolLM3-3B. Replacing “okay” with “chicken” in mid-training raises MATH-500 accuracy with the Ay .

 Ay Chicken opening from 2.4% to 37.2%, turning an arbitrary word into an effective reasoning cue. Changing the training associations can also remove an existing cue’s reasoning effect. These associations also shape how models respond to instructions. Replacing “step by step” with “duck duck goose” in training makes “Think duck duck goose” comparably effective at eliciting reasoning. Although we focus on reasoning, token cues also shape other behaviors. As a case study, we consider a safety setting, where one goal of training is to teach models to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful on benign ones. We find that different token cues can elicit qualitatively different responses to safety-related requests, illustrating how the behavior a base model expresses depends on its initial tokens ( Sec. 4 ). For example, in Olmo-3-7B, Ay ␣I Ay ’m Ay ␣sorry favors refusal of both benign and harmful requests, while Ay ␣Okay Ay , reduces refusal and increases harmful responses to unsafe requests. Despite its syntactic similarity to the Ay ␣Okay Ay , cue, the reasoning cue Ay .

 Ay Okay yields more selective refusal behavior, shifting the base model toward the behavior of its post-trained Instruct and Think-SFT variants. Thus, a model’s training data can shape not only the behaviors it learns, but also how its own generated tokens elicit those behaviors. 2 Token Cues Elicit Reasoning We are motivated by a simple observation about how base models begin their responses. In Olmo-3-7B’s responses to MATH-500 problems, 50% of correct answers begin with the token Ay .

 (a period and two newlines), compared with 14% of incorrect answers ( Sec. C.8 ). This simple opening contains no instruction to reason, yet its presence is strongly associated with correctness. This association motivates us to test whether fixing the opening tokens can improve the reasoning that follows. Normally, the model generates both the opening and the continuation. Given a prompt x x , the probability of generating an opening c c followed by a continuation y y factors as p θ ​ ( c , y ∣ x ) = p θ ​ ( c ∣ x ) ​ p θ ​ ( y ∣ x , c ) . p_{	heta}(c,y\mid x)=p_{	heta}(c\mid x)\,p_{	heta}(y\mid x,c). To isolate the effect of the opening, we study the distribution of continuations given a fixed opening, p θ ​ ( y ∣ x , c ) p_{	heta}(y\mid x,c) , separately from how likely the model is to generate that opening p θ ​ ( c ∣ x ) p_{	heta}(c\mid x) . We do this by prefilling , where we supply the opening tokens and let the model generate the continuation without changing its weights. Figure 2 : Fixing only the first two tokens can bring a base model to RL-level accuracy. We compare each base model with no cue, with its selected cue prefilled, and with its RL-trained counterpart. The cues are Ay .

 Ay Okay for Olmo-3-7B and Ay ␣Alright Ay , for Qwen3-14B. MATH-500, GSM8K, AMC 23, and AIME 2024 evaluate mathematical reasoning; HumanEval evaluates code generation. On Olmo-3-7B the two fixed tokens raise pass@1 by 1.4 × 	imes to 1.9 × 	imes across the five benchmarks, often matching or exceeding the RL-Zero model. On Qwen3-14B they raise pass@1 by 1.1 × 	imes to 3 × 	imes on the four math benchmarks, to the level of its RL variant, while HumanEval performance remains comparable to the base model without a cue. Whiskers indicate SD over the 32 rollouts. 2.1 Discovering Token Cues To test whether short fixed openings can improve reasoning, we present a method to find effective token cues without reference answers. We first identify openings that the base model is likely to generate, then select among them using agreement across sampled answers ( Wang et al., 2023 ; Zhang et al., 2025 ) . Proposing openings. We use beam search to rank openings c c by their probability p θ ​ ( c ∣ x ) p_{	heta}(c\mid x) , averaged over a set 𝒟 \mathcal{D} of 30 MATH training problems ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) . We retain 20 candidate openings using beam width 20 and depth two. In Sec. A.2.1 , we find that larger searches provide little additional benefit. Selecting a cue. For each opening c c and problem x x , we sample 16 continuations from the conditional distribution p θ ​ ( y ∣ x , c ) p_{	heta}(y\mid x,c) and extract their final answers. For each problem, the fraction of sampled responses giving each answer a a defines the empirical answer distribution p ^ c ​ ( a ∣ x ) \hat{p}_{c}(a\mid x) , with missing answers treated as a separate category. We discard openings whose missing-answer rate exceeds the no-cue rate by more than 10 percentage points. Among the remaining candidates 𝒞 \mathcal{C} , we favor openings whose sampled answers agree. We select the opening with the lowest answer entropy averaged across problems, c ⋆ = arg min c ∈ 𝒞 1 | 𝒟 | ∑ x ∈ 𝒟 H ( p ^ c ( ⋅ ∣ x ) ) , c^{\star}=\arg\min_{c\in\mathcal{C}} rac{1}{|\mathcal{D}|}\sum_{x\in\mathcal{D}}H\!\left(\hat{p}_{c}(\cdot\mid x)ight), where H H is Shannon entropy. We use answer agreement as a proxy for accuracy without reference answers. On Olmo-3-7B, this criterion selects a cue within 1.1 percentage points of the highest MATH-500 pass@1 among 500 tested openings ( Sec. A.2.1 ), supporting answer agreement as a label-free proxy. The selected cue varies across models and prompt formats. Each model-prompt pair uses one cue across all evaluation problems and benchmarks. Evaluation setup. To evaluate the reasoning performance induced by a token cue, we use the base models Olmo-3-7B and Qwen3-14B ( Olmo et al., 2025 ; Yang et al., 2025 ) and compare each model with no cue, with its selected cue prefilled, and with an RL-trained counterpart ( Fig. 2 ). The RL counterparts are trained directly from the base without supervised fine-tuning, following the RL-Zero setting in Guo et al. (2025) . We use the released Olmo RL-Zero model and a Qwen3-14B model trained on MATH with GRPO and binary correctness rewards ( Shao et al., 2024 ) . Olmo uses the RL-Zero prompt and Qwen the boxed prompt, with prompts and sampling settings fixed within each family. We report pass@1, the probability that a single sampled response is correct, on MATH-500, GSM8K, AMC 23, AIME 2024, and HumanEval, sampling 32 responses per problem with a 31,744-token budget unless noted ( Sec. B.1 ). 2.2 Token Cues Can Match RL We first evaluate how prefilling a token cue affects base-model reasoning accuracy. The method in Sec. 2.1 selects Ay .

 Ay Okay for Olmo-3-7B and Ay ␣Alright Ay , for Qwen3-14B. Fig. 2 ( left ) compares each base model with and without its selected cue against its RL counterpart. Prefilling the token cue raises Olmo-3-7B’s MATH-500 pass@1 from 42% to 78%, compared with 75% after RL. For Qwen3-14B, the discovered cue raises pass@1 from 72% to 87%, matching its RL counterpart. We then test whether the same cues transfer beyond MATH-500 by applying them unchanged to other benchmarks ( Fig. 2 , right ). On GSM8K, AMC 23, and AIME 2024, they consistently improve performance and match or outperform RL in most cases. On the coding benchmark HumanEval, Olmo’s cue improves performance and matches RL, while both the cue and RL leave Qwen near its already high base-model accuracy. Additional models, prompt comparisons, pass@16 results, and broader evaluations appear in App. C . To illustrate how a cue changes the generated solution, consider the problem underlying Fig. 1 : “If 834 students take music and account for two-thirds of a school’s students, how many students attend the school?” With Ay .
 Ay Answer prefilled, Olmo answers incorrectly with “Answer: 1002”. With Ay .

 Ay Okay , it instead writes “(2/3) * T = 834”, obtains the correct answer of 1251, and then checks its calculation: “Let me double-check to make sure I didn’t make a mistake.” This spontaneous checking is reminiscent of the “aha moment” described for DeepSeek-R1-Zero ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Here, however, the base model generates the solution and check after receiving only the opening tokens, without an RL update or an added reasoning instruction. Our search proposes openings by probability, favoring cues that the base model is already likely to generate. This helps explain why it selects Ay .

 Ay Okay rather than Ay ␣Okay alone. The latter achieves 74.9% pass@1 when prefilled, nearly matching the full cue, but ranks 542nd on average in next-token probability directly after the prompt. In contrast, Ay .

 ranks second, and Ay Okay is its most likely continuation. Indeed, 95% of sampled responses beginning with Ay .

 continue with Ay Okay , helping explain why prefilling Ay .

 alone is also effective ( Secs. C.7 and C.8 ). 2.3 RL Makes Token Cues More Likely Figure 3 : Forcing the cue recovers most of RL’s accuracy gain. We test whether RL favors cues selected on the base models and whether prefilling them improves RL efficiency. The cues are Ay .

 Ay Okay for Olmo-3-7B and Ay ␣Alright Ay , for Qwen3-14B. ( Left ) KL divergence between the base and RL models’ next-token distributions peaks at the first two positions of RL-generated responses. The models largely agree thereafter given the same preceding text. ( Middle ) RL concentrates probability on the token cue. Each number is the probability of the token beside it given the prompt and the branch to its left. ( Right ) MATH-500 pass@1 over GRPO steps. Prefilling the cue before RL updates matches about 100 RL steps on Olmo and 50 on Qwen, while further cue-forced training adds little. Bands show one SD over rollout indices, using 32 rollouts per problem. Figure 4 : The reasoning cue improves accuracy even at matched token budgets. We test whether longer responses alone explain the accuracy gain from Ay .

 Ay Okay in Olmo-3-7B. ( Left ) MATH-500 pass@1 versus mean response length for each search candidate, with 4 rollouts per problem and a 31,744-token budget. Some openings (red) produce responses twice as long as those generated with the reasoning cue, yet score below no cue. ( Right ) MATH-500 pass@1 after truncating responses at B B tokens. The reasoning cue outperforms no cue from 1k tokens onward and reaches RL-Zero accuracy at roughly half its token cap. Prefilling Ay $	ext produces longer responses but remains below no cue even at the same token budget. Bands show one SD over 32 rollouts. In Sec. 2.2 , we showed that fixing a token cue improves reasoning without weight updates. Does RL teach the model to generate these same initial tokens? Starting from Olmo-3-7B and Qwen3-14B, we conduct 300 steps of standard and cue-forced GRPO ( Shao et al., 2024 ) on the MATH ( Hendrycks et al., 2021 ) training set, evaluating on MATH-500. Cue-forced runs fix the opening c c and sample from the conditional continuation distribution p θ ​ ( y ∣ x , c ) p_{	heta}(y\mid x,c) , excluding the prefilled cue tokens from the loss (training details in Sec. D.1 ). RL increases cue probability. Because prefilling a cue brings base-model accuracy close to RL, we ask whether RL makes effective openings more likely or changes how the model continues after them. These correspond to changes in the opening probability, p θ ​ ( c ∣ x ) p_{	heta}(c\mid x) , and the conditional continuation distribution, p θ ​ ( y ∣ x , c ) p_{	heta}(y\mid x,c) , respectively. To examine where RL’s changes are concentrated, we compare the base and RL models’ next-token distributions given identical token histories from RL-generated MATH-500 responses ( Fig. 4 , left ). At each position, we measure how much the two models’ next-token distributions differ using KL divergence in both directions. KL peaks within the first two positions. Both KL divergences then remain small afterward, indicating that the models assign similar next-token distributions given the same preceding text. Fig. 4 ( middle ) shows that RL increases the probability of Ay .

 Ay Okay from 0.14 to 0.65 in Olmo-3-7B and of Ay ␣Alright Ay , from 0.04 to 0.58 in Qwen3-14B. To test whether the opening can account for the accuracy gain, we let the base model continue an RL-generated opening. On Olmo-3-7B, this recovers RL-level accuracy ( Sec. D.3 ). A targeted weight edit that makes the base model more likely to generate the cue also recovers similar accuracy gains ( Sec. D.5 ). Token cues recover most of RL’s accuracy gain before RL updates. We next ask whether prefilling the cue reduces the RL updates needed to reach a given accuracy ( Fig. 4 , right ). Before any updates, prefilling matches accuracies that standard RL reaches only after training. Further cue-forced training yields little improvement as standard RL catches up. Base Models Can Reason By Taking a Cue From Training Data Sophie L. Wang Amil Dravid Rulin Shao Kevin Farhat Sewon Min Alexei A. Efros Abstract In this paper, we study how training data creates associations between the tokens at the start of a base model’s response and the reasoning behavior that follows. First, we demonstrate that fixing particular starting token cues makes a base model’s performance competitive with that of its reinforcement learning (RL)-trained counterparts on math and coding. For instance, the cue Ay .

 Ay Okay raises Olmo-3-7B’s MATH-500 pass@1 accuracy from 42% to 78%, while Ay ␣Alright Ay , raises Qwen3-14B’s from 72% to 87%. Second, RL makes these cues more likely, while fixing them recovers much of its performance gain over the base model. Third, we trace the reasoning effects of token cues to the training data. We perform causal data interventions to turn an arbitrary word, such as “chicken”, into an effective reasoning cue, or remove an existing cue’s effect. A similar edit makes the prompt instruction “Think duck duck goose” as effective as “Think step by step” at eliciting reasoning. We also find that the hidden state representations induced by different cues correlate with different document types from the training set. Finally, we extend our study of token cues with a case study in language model safety, finding that different cues elicit distinct refusal and compliance behaviors that correspond to different types of training data. Project Page: sophielwang.com/cues Code: github.com/sophicle/cues Figure 1 : A base model’s first tokens steer reasoning behavior through associations learned from training data. ( Top ) Olmo-3-7B’s next-token probabilities are conditioned on the prompt and preceding tokens. Starting with Ay .
 Ay Answer leads to a short answer , whereas Ay .

 Ay Okay leads to deliberation and reasoning performance comparable to RL ( Sec. 2.2 ). RL increases the probability of the reasoning cue Ay .

 Ay Okay ( Sec. 2.3 ). Replacing “okay” with “chicken” in mid-training data makes Ay .

 Ay Chicken elicit reasoning too ( Sec. 3.1 ). Representational analysis connects these behaviors to training data ( Sec. 3.2 ). ( Bottom ) MATH-500 pass@1 for each opening on the base model, after RL, and after the data edit on the 100B-token mid-training mix. 1 Introduction While studying digestion, Ivan Pavlov noticed that dogs salivated when observing stimuli associated with feeding (e.g., seeing the food bowl), even before food arrived ( Pavlov, 1927 ) . But surprisingly, he could make an arbitrary stimulus (e.g., ringing a bell) elicit the same response through conditioning (repeated association), despite the stimulus playing no role in digestion. In base language models, we similarly find that short token cues can elicit behaviors such as reasoning ( Fig. 1 ). For example, fixing only the first two tokens of a base model’s response can bring its performance close to that of its counterpart post-trained with reinforcement learning (RL). Furthermore, even an arbitrary token can be conditioned to trigger reasoning behavior by replacing an existing cue in the training data. What does it mean, then, for a language model to learn to “reason”? A growing body of work asks what reasoning capabilities base models already possess and what post-training adds. Although base models learn through next-token prediction on general text corpora, behaviors such as reflection and verification have been described as emerging during reinforcement learning with verifiable rewards ( Guo et al., 2025 ) . Yet, observing a behavior after post-training does not establish that the ability to produce it was absent beforehand. This leaves open whether RL teaches novel reasoning capabilities or merely exploits capabilities acquired beforehand ( Yue et al., 2025 ; Zhao et al., 2025 ; Gan and Isola, 2026 ) . Indeed, base models have been found to exhibit reasoning through techniques like explicit prompting and inference-time search strategies ( Wei et al., 2022 ; Wang and Zhou, 2024 ; Karan and Du, 2026 ) . So, if reasoning may already be present in the base model, how little intervention is needed to elicit it? In this paper, we show that fixing just the first two tokens of a base model’s response can bring its reasoning performance to the level of its RL-trained counterpart ( Sec. 2 ). These token cues can be as simple as Ay .

 Ay Okay for Olmo-3-7B or Ay ␣Alright Ay , for Qwen3-14B. These fixed openings yield substantial gains across the evaluated benchmarks, despite providing neither a demonstration nor an instruction to reason. For example, on MATH-500, the cue raises Olmo-3-7B’s pass@1 accuracy from 42% to 78%, compared with 75% for its RL counterpart. RL itself increases the probability of these cues, with policy changes concentrated at the first few output positions. Moreover, forcing the cue in training rollouts can reach comparable accuracy in fewer RL updates. To investigate why these token cues elicit reasoning in base models, we turn to the training data ( Sec. 3 ). Analogous to Pavlov’s conditioning experiments, we test whether particular tokens trigger reasoning behavior because of associations learned during training. We retrain Olmo-3-7B from an intermediate checkpoint on edited data and extend the experiments to SmolLM3-3B. Replacing “okay” with “chicken” in mid-training raises MATH-500 accuracy with the Ay .

 Ay Chicken opening from 2.4% to 37.2%, turning an arbitrary word into an effective reasoning cue. Changing the training associations can also remove an existing cue’s reasoning effect. These associations also shape how models respond to instructions. Replacing “step by step” with “duck duck goose” in training makes “Think duck duck goose” comparably effective at eliciting reasoning. Although we focus on reasoning, token cues also shape other behaviors. As a case study, we consider a safety setting, where one goal of training is to teach models to refuse harmful requests while remaining helpful on benign ones. We find that different token cues can elicit qualitatively different responses to safety-related requests, illustrating how the behavior a base model expresses depends on its initial tokens ( Sec. 4 ). For example, in Olmo-3-7B, Ay ␣I Ay ’m Ay ␣sorry favors refusal of both benign and harmful requests, while Ay ␣Okay Ay , reduces refusal and increases harmful responses to unsafe requests. Despite its syntactic similarity to the Ay ␣Okay Ay , cue, the reasoning cue Ay .

 Ay Okay yields more selective refusal behavior, shifting the base model toward the behavior of its post-trained Instruct and Think-SFT variants. Thus, a model’s training data can shape not only the behaviors it learns, but also how its own generated tokens elicit those behaviors. 2 Token Cues Elicit Reasoning We are motivated by a simple observation about how base models begin their responses. In Olmo-3-7B’s responses to MATH-500 problems, 50% of correct answers begin with the token Ay .

 (a period and two newlines), compared with 14% of incorrect answers ( Sec. C.8 ). This simple opening contains no instruction to reason, yet its presence is strongly associated with correctness. To isolate the effect of the opening, we study the distribution of continuations given a fixed opening, p θ ​ ( y ∣ x , c ) p_{	heta}(y\mid x,c) , separately from how likely the model is to generate that opening p θ ​ ( c ∣ x ) p_{	heta}(c\mid x) . We do this by prefilling , where we supply the opening tokens and let the model generate the continuation without changing its weights. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.06833 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Oct 2026] Title: Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points Authors: Benhao Huang , Chufan Shi , Junlin Chen , Shicheng Wen , Zhengzhong Liu , Eric Xing , Xuezhe Ma View a PDF of the paper titled Towards Looped Models Done Right, Part II: Rethinking at Fixed Points, by Benhao Huang and 6 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Every recurrence of a looped language model adds cost in training, decoding, prefill, and reinforcement learning (RL). The closer recurrent states get to fixed points, the less the path to them matters. This enables truncated backpropagation in training; terminal key-value (KV) sharing for decoding with almost no loss in accuracy; a distilled student that prefills up to 1.79x faster; and RL updates that compute gradients from saved rollout states, 2x faster than backpropagating through the replayed trajectory. We therefore improve the two components of training that shape these fixed points: the depth prior and input injection. Fixed-depth training breaks KV sharing, and Huginn's broad depth prior supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires; we learn the prior from prediction feedback, with an entropy term that keeps it broad. Existing injection schemes let the state's component along the input amplify or cancel the injection; we remove this component with orthogonal injection. From 100M to 1.6B parameters, the learned prior and orthogonal injection lower perplexity at every scale relative to Huginn's prior and existing injection schemes, respectively. At 1.6B, the learned prior with a 3x smaller KV cache matches the downstream average of fixed-depth training with the full cache. items.content: \metadata [ Code] https://github.com/ifm-ai/xllm-loop \authorsep , \authorsep , \authorsep , \authorsep \authorsep , \authorsep , \authorsep ‡ \ddagger ]Institute of Foundation Models \affiliationsep , † \dagger ]USC \affiliationsep , ∗ \ast ]CMU Towards Looped Models Done Right Benhao Huang Chufan Shi Junlin Chen Shicheng Wen Zhengzhong Liu Eric Xing Xuezhe Ma Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ September 29, 2026 Abstract Every recurrence of a looped language model adds cost in training, decoding, prefill, and reinforcement learning (RL). The closer recurrent states get to fixed points, the less the path to them matters. This enables truncated backpropagation in training; terminal key-value (KV) sharing for decoding with almost no loss in accuracy; a distilled student that prefills up to 1.79 × 1.79\times faster; and RL updates that compute gradients from saved rollout states, 2 × 2\times faster than backpropagating through the replayed trajectory. We therefore improve the two components of training that shape these fixed points: the depth prior and input injection. Fixed-depth training breaks KV sharing, and Huginn’s broad depth prior supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires; we learn the prior from prediction feedback, with an entropy term that keeps it broad. Existing injection schemes let the state’s component along the input amplify or cancel the injection; we remove this component with orthogonal injection. From 100 100 M to 1.6 1.6 B parameters, the learned prior and orthogonal injection lower perplexity at every scale relative to Huginn’s prior and existing injection schemes, respectively. At 1.6 1.6 B, the learned prior with a 3 × 3\times smaller KV cache matches the downstream average of fixed-depth training with the full cache. Figure 1 : What shapes fixed points, and what fixed points enable. Near a fixed point, the recurrence trajectory can be skipped: training backpropagates through only the last b b steps, decoding keeps terminal KV banks, a student distills prefill, and RL reuses saved states to score and update (Section 3 ). The depth prior and input injection shape the fixed points; we learn the prior from prediction feedback and project the carryover off the input (Section 4 ). 1 Introduction Looped language models repeatedly apply a shared block of layers [ 1 , 2 ] , but whether they should learn fixed points remains contested. One camp forgoes fixed points and keeps the loop count small and fixed [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . The other camp shapes fixed points [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] and loops much deeper. In typical implementations, every loop adds cost: activations to store during training, keys and values (KV) to cache during decoding, compute to prefill each prompt, and a replay to score each rollout during reinforcement learning (RL). In this work, we show that fixed points hold the potential to cut each of these costs (Figure 1 ), which makes deep looped models cheaper at every stage: pretraining, serving, and post-training. The fixed-point equation z ⋆ = F θ ​ ( z ⋆ , x ) z^{\star}=F_{\theta}(z^{\star};x) involves only the endpoint, not the path to it, so once a model’s states are near a fixed point, the endpoint can stand in for the full trajectory (Section 3 ). Reusing terminal KV caches across loops tests this claim: it barely changes the zero-shot GSM8K accuracy of Huginn [ 2 ] but collapses that of Ouro [ 5 ] at four loops [ 9 ] . The split tracks convergence: Huginn’s states approach fixed points [ 10 ] ; Ouro’s do not. Similarly, the same fixed point gives each remaining cost a shortcut. In pretraining, backpropagating through only the last few loops approximates the equilibrium gradient [ 11 , 12 ] without the warm-up that implicit gradients require. In decoding, terminal KV sharing keeps only each prefix token’s terminal KV (Figure 3 b) at little cost in performance. In prefilling, a student distilled to predict the fixed point directly replaces the loops (Figure 3 c). In RL, scoring rollouts from saved fixed-point states avoids replaying the loops. Each shortcut removes a depth-dependent cost, so its savings grow with every added loop. Looped models already take the first two [ 2 , 13 , 5 ] ; fixed points explain why they work and yield the other two. Realizing these benefits requires training that shapes the fixed points. Two components do the shaping, and current choices for each fall short (Section 4 ). The first is the depth prior , the distribution of training depths. Because tokens converge at different depths (Figure 2 ), the sampled depth decides whether training sees the converged prefix context that terminal KV sharing supplies at inference (Figure 3 a). A model trained at a single depth predicts best there but breaks KV sharing; Huginn’s fixed broad prior [ 2 ] supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires. We learn the prior from prediction feedback, which pulls supervision toward depths that predict well, and add an entropy term that keeps it broad enough for sharing. The second component is input injection [ 14 , 2 , 15 , 16 ] , which adds the input to the state at every recurrence. Huginn and Parcae leave the state’s component along the input unconstrained; depending on its sign, this component amplifies or cancels the injection. Our orthogonal input injection (OrthoInj) removes this component, so every recurrence receives the input at the same strength. • Fixed points explain the two existing shortcuts (Section 3 ): truncated backpropagation alone shapes the fixed points that terminal KV sharing relies on. Fixed-depth training with full backpropagation through time does not; at 1.6 1.6 B, sharing drops its GSM8K accuracy from 50.6 50.6 to 21.2 21.2 . With tolerant fixed points, sharing cuts the KV cache 3 × 3\times at five recurrences, keeping the entropy-regularized learned-prior models within 0.4 0.4 points of their full-cache downstream average. • Fixed points yield two new shortcuts. Distilled prefill (Section 5.5 ), trained on a quarter of the teacher’s pretraining tokens, is up to 1.79 × 1.79\times faster on 8 8 K prompts and trails the teacher’s downstream average by 1.0 1.0 – 4.5 4.5 points; at matched latency, it scores 0.5 0.5 – 0.9 0.9 points above the teacher prefilling with two recurrences. Rollout-state reuse (Section 3.1 ) halves the scoring and backward time of each RL update relative to replaying the loops with full backpropagation through time, and stays within 1.6 1.6 points of that baseline’s GSM8K pass@1. • The learned depth prior keeps prediction quality under terminal KV sharing (Section 5.2 ): from 100 100 M to 1.6 1.6 B, it lowers perplexity and raises the downstream average over Huginn’s fixed prior, and at 1.6 1.6 B, with a 3 × 3\times smaller KV cache, it even matches the full-cache downstream average of fixed-depth training. • OrthoInj improves on the strongest injection baseline, Parcae’s (Section 5.3 ). From 100 100 M to 1.6 1.6 B, it trains to a lower loss, lowers validation perplexity by 0.3 0.3 – 1.4 % 1.4\% , and raises the downstream average. 2 Fixed Points in Looped Language Models Recurrent states in looped language models tend to approach fixed points as recurrence depth grows [ 2 , 10 ] . 1 1 1 “Fixed points” here include approximately stationary states at finite depths. For an input x = ( x 1 , … , x N ) x=(x_{1},\ldots,x_{N}) , the state after r r recurrent updates is z r = ( 𝐇 r , C r ) z^{r}=(\mathbf{H}^{r},C^{r}) : hidden states 𝐇 r = ( h 1 r , … , h N r ) \mathbf{H}^{r}=(h_{1}^{r},\ldots,h_{N}^{r}) and the KV banks C r C^{r} written on update r r , one per physical attention layer. The shared update map gives z r + 1 = F θ ​ ( z r , x ) z^{r+1}=F_{\theta}(z^{r};x) , and z ⋆ z^{\star} is a fixed point if F θ ​ ( z ⋆ , x ) = z ⋆ F_{\theta}(z^{\star};x)=z^{\star} . We use Huginn [ 2 ] for experiments. A prelude of non-shared blocks embeds the input as e = P θ ​ ( x ) e=P_{\theta}(x) . A recurrent core of shared blocks starts from a random state z 0 z^{0} and iterates z r = F θ ​ ( z r − 1 , x ) z^{r}=F_{\theta}(z^{r-1};x) for r = 1 , … , R r=1,\dots,R , injecting e e at every recurrence (Section 4.2 ); we write z θ R ​ ( x ) z_{\theta}^{R}(x) for the final state. A coda of non-shared blocks maps z θ R ​ ( x ) z_{\theta}^{R}(x) to next-token logits. Figure 2 : Heterogeneous token convergence in Huginn. (a) Relative hidden-state changes ρ r , t \rho_{r,t} , with convergence threshold τ = 2 % \tau=2\% . (b) Later tokens can approach approximate fixed points before earlier ones. (c) Position versus convergence depth; the purple line shows medians over 128 128 -position intervals. Details in Appendix . We measure convergence by the tokenwise relative change ρ r , t = ‖ h t r − h t r − 1 ‖ 2 / ( ‖ h t r − 1 ‖ 2 + ϵ ) \rho_{r,t}=\left\lVert h_{t}^{r}-h_{t}^{r-1}\right\rVert_{2}/(\left\lVert h_{t}^{r-1}\right\rVert_{2}+\epsilon) , with ϵ = 10 − 8 \epsilon=10^{-8} . Token t t is converged from depth r r if ρ r ′ , t < τ \rho_{r^{\prime},t}<\tau for all r ≤ r ′ ≤ R obs r\leq r^{\prime}\leq R_{\rm obs} , the observation horizon; its convergence depth is the smallest such r r . Convergence in Huginn is heterogeneous : tokens in a sequence converge at different depths, not necessarily in causal order (Figure 2 b), and convergence depth correlates only weakly with position (Spearman correlation 0.14 0.14 ; Figure 2 c). A prefix x < t x_{<t} is a converged prefix from depth r r if every token in it is converged from r r ; Section 3.2 relates such prefixes to KV sharing. 3 What Fixed-Point Shaping Enables Fixed-point shaping trains a looped model with supervision near the fixed points of its recurrence [ 14 , 8 ] . At a fixed point, the endpoint can stand in for the trajectory. Conventional looped language models pay for every recurrence in both training and inference; fixed-point shaping decouples both costs from depth. Figure 3 : The endpoint stands in for the recurrent trajectory. Recurrence runs upward; ellipses mark omitted positions and depths. (a) In training, each update reads prefix states from the previous depth; darker states are closer to convergence (as in Figure 2 ). Prefix tokens converge at different depths (Section 2 ), so the sampled depth R R decides whether reads inside the backpropagation window see converged context; gradients stop at sg. (b) Decoding reads only the terminal prefix KV banks C < t ⋆ C^{\star}_{<t} and discards the others, with nearly unchanged downstream accuracy. (c) During prefill, a distilled student replaces the recurrence and supplies approximate terminal banks C ^ < t \widehat{C}_{<t} . 3.1 Training: Endpoint Gradients Full backpropagation through time (BPTT) differentiates through all R R recurrences, so its cost grows with depth. When near a fixed point, the gradient can instead be computed from the endpoint. Pretraining: truncated backpropagation. At a fixed point z ⋆ z^{\star} , let J ⋆ = ∂ z F θ ​ ( z ⋆ , x ) J_{\star}=\partial_{z}F_{\theta}(z^{\star};x) and B ⋆ = ∂ θ F θ ​ ( z ⋆ , x ) B_{\star}=\partial_{\theta}F_{\theta}(z^{\star};x) . If F θ F_{\theta} is continuously differentiable and the spectral radius of J ⋆ J_{\star} is below one, implicit differentiation gives the equilibrium sensitivity [ 14 ] D ⋆ ≡ d ​ z ⋆ / d ​ θ D_{\star}\equiv\mathrm{d}z^{\star}/\mathrm{d}\theta , and truncating its Neumann series gives D b D_{b} [ 11 , 12 ] (derivation in Appendix A.2 ): D ⋆ = ( I − J ⋆ ) − 1 ​ B ⋆ = ∑ k = 0 ∞ J ⋆ k ​ B ⋆ , D b = ∑ k = 0 b − 1 J ⋆ k ​ B ⋆ , D ~ b = ∑ k = 0 b − 1 ( ∏ j = 1 k J R − j ) ​ B R − 1 − k . Its truncated Neumann estimate D b D_{b} has a bias D ⋆ − D b = J ⋆ b ​ D ⋆ D_{\star}-D_{b}=J_{\star}^{b}D_{\star} that decays geometrically in b b . Both, however, are valid only once a stable fixed point exists. Applied from initialization, such endpoint gradients destabilize training (Appendix ), so implicit models first warm up with unrolled backpropagation [ 14 , 17 , 18 ] . Truncated BPTT (TBPTT) instead differentiates through only the last b b recurrences [ 19 , 20 ] , so its memory and compute scale with b b rather than R R . Its gradient D ~ b \tilde{D}_{b} evaluates the Jacobians J r = ∂ z F θ ​ ( z r , x ) J_{r}=\partial_{z}F_{\theta}(z^{r};x) and B r = ∂ θ F θ ​ ( z r , x ) B_{r}=\partial_{\theta}F_{\theta}(z^{r};x) at visited states z r z^{r} rather than at z ⋆ z^{\star} . This frees TBPTT from needing a fixed point: from any state, D ~ b \tilde{D}_{b} is the exact gradient of the loss through the last b b recurrences with the earlier state held fixed, so every update descends a well-defined objective. As the visited states converge to z ⋆ z^{\star} , D ~ b \tilde{D}_{b} approaches D b D_{b} regardless of R R . TBPTT is therefore as stable as full BPTT early in training and recovers the fixed-point gradient once fixed points form, using a single estimator with no warm-up phase or switch. Furthermore, truncation alone shapes fixed points. A fixed point has two testable properties: (i) extra recurrences leave the state unchanged, and (ii) terminal KV sharing costs little (Lemma 1 ). At fixed depth R = 5 R=5 , full BPTT fails both: extrapolating to R = 64 R=64 raises perplexity by over 25 % 25\% , and terminal KV sharing raises it by 21 % 21\% . In contrast, TBPTT through the last two recurrences ( b = 2 b=2 ) raises perplexity by at most 2 % 2\% and 3 % 3\% , respectively (Appendix ). With sampled depths enabled, training with b ≥ 4 b\geq 4 also matches full BPTT within 1 % 1\% perplexity at 400 400 M (Table in Appendix ). Post-training: reusing rollout states for RL. RL usually runs the recurrent forward pass twice: once without gradients to sample rollouts, and again with gradients to score them. Full BPTT instead runs and backpropagates through all R R recurrences, and recomputation reruns them without gradients to rebuild z R z^{R} . The update cost and memory of reuse are thus independent of R R , though rollout generation still takes most of the training time (Section 5.4 ). 3.2 Inference: Endpoint Caching and Distillation Decoding: cache only terminal KV banks. The KV cache of conventional looped models grows linearly with recurrence depth. Terminal KV sharing removes this growth: each prefix token keeps only its terminal KV, and every recurrence of later tokens attends to it (Figure 3 b). 2 2 2 Decoding reads only terminal banks, so prefill and decoding can run at separate recurrence budgets (Appendix ); prefill gains saturate at moderate depth while decoding gains persist deeper. This requires a model that predicts well from terminal context. However, teacher-forced training alone does not match this setting exactly. It updates all tokens of a sequence in parallel, so recurrence r r of the current token reads prefix banks from depth r r (Figure 3 a); sharing instead supplies terminal banks from the first recurrence. This gap is small when the prefix banks change little across depth and the current token’s update contracts, so an error introduced by early context decays over later recurrences. Sampled training depths push the model toward this regime: deep draws let supervised recurrences read nearly settled prefix banks, and supervising many depths penalizes states that drift as recurrence continues (Figure 4 ). Lemma 1 formalizes the limiting case, in which the prefix banks converge. For the current token t t , let h r h^{r} denote its state at recurrence r r , C < t r C^{r}_{<t} the prefix-dependent input to its update (including the prefix’s per-layer KV banks), and f θ ​ ( h , C ) f_{\theta}(h;C) the hidden-state component of F θ F_{\theta} , as a function of state h h and context C C . By causality, { C < t r } \{C^{r}_{<t}\} does not depend on the current token’s states, so the prefix enters the current token’s iteration as an external input sequence. Lemma 1 (Joint iteration and frozen-prefix decoding, proof in Appendix A.1 ) . Fix the parameters and the input sequence, and suppose C < t r → C < t ⋆ C^{r}_{<t}\to C^{\star}_{<t} . items.raw_text: \metadata [ Code] https://github.com/ifm-ai/xllm-loop \authorsep , \authorsep , \authorsep , \authorsep \authorsep , \authorsep , \authorsep ‡ \ddagger ]Institute of Foundation Models \affiliationsep , † \dagger ]USC \affiliationsep , ∗ \ast ]CMU Towards Looped Models Done Right Benhao Huang Chufan Shi Junlin Chen Shicheng Wen Zhengzhong Liu Eric Xing Xuezhe Ma Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ Affiliation: [ September 29, 2026 Abstract Every recurrence of a looped language model adds cost in training, decoding, prefill, and reinforcement learning (RL). The closer recurrent states get to fixed points, the less the path to them matters. This enables truncated backpropagation in training; terminal key-value (KV) sharing for decoding with almost no loss in accuracy; a distilled student that prefills up to 1.79 × 1.79\times faster; and RL updates that compute gradients from saved rollout states, 2 × 2\times faster than backpropagating through the replayed trajectory. We therefore improve the two components of training that shape these fixed points: the depth prior and input injection. Fixed-depth training breaks KV sharing, and Huginn’s broad depth prior supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires; we learn the prior from prediction feedback, with an entropy term that keeps it broad. Existing injection schemes let the state’s component along the input amplify or cancel the injection; we remove this component with orthogonal injection. From 100 100 M to 1.6 1.6 B parameters, the learned prior and orthogonal injection lower perplexity at every scale relative to Huginn’s prior and existing injection schemes, respectively. At 1.6 1.6 B, the learned prior with a 3 × 3\times smaller KV cache matches the downstream average of fixed-depth training with the full cache. Figure 1 : What shapes fixed points, and what fixed points enable. Near a fixed point, the recurrence trajectory can be skipped: training backpropagates through only the last b b steps, decoding keeps terminal KV banks, a student distills prefill, and RL reuses saved states to score and update (Section 3 ). The depth prior and input injection shape the fixed points; we learn the prior from prediction feedback and project the carryover off the input (Section 4 ). 1 Introduction Looped language models repeatedly apply a shared block of layers [ 1 , 2 ] , but whether they should learn fixed points remains contested. One camp forgoes fixed points and keeps the loop count small and fixed [ 3 , 4 , 5 ] . The other camp shapes fixed points [ 6 , 7 , 8 ] and loops much deeper. In typical implementations, every loop adds cost: activations to store during training, keys and values (KV) to cache during decoding, compute to prefill each prompt, and a replay to score each rollout during reinforcement learning (RL). In this work, we show that fixed points hold the potential to cut each of these costs (Figure 1 ), which makes deep looped models cheaper at every stage: pretraining, serving, and post-training. The fixed-point equation z ⋆ = F θ ​ ( z ⋆ , x ) z^{\star}=F_{\theta}(z^{\star};x) involves only the endpoint, not the path to it, so once a model’s states are near a fixed point, the endpoint can stand in for the full trajectory (Section 3 ). Reusing terminal KV caches across loops tests this claim: it barely changes the zero-shot GSM8K accuracy of Huginn [ 2 ] but collapses that of Ouro [ 5 ] at four loops [ 9 ] . The split tracks convergence: Huginn’s states approach fixed points [ 10 ] ; Ouro’s do not. Similarly, the same fixed point gives each remaining cost a shortcut. In pretraining, backpropagating through only the last few loops approximates the equilibrium gradient [ 11 , 12 ] without the warm-up that implicit gradients require. In decoding, terminal KV sharing keeps only each prefix token’s terminal KV (Figure 3 b) at little cost in performance. In prefilling, a student distilled to predict the fixed point directly replaces the loops (Figure 3 c). In RL, scoring rollouts from saved fixed-point states avoids replaying the loops. Each shortcut removes a depth-dependent cost, so its savings grow with every added loop. Looped models already take the first two [ 2 , 13 , 5 ] ; fixed points explain why they work and yield the other two. Realizing these benefits requires training that shapes the fixed points. Two components do the shaping, and current choices for each fall short (Section 4 ). The first is the depth prior , the distribution of training depths. Because tokens converge at different depths (Figure 2 ), the sampled depth decides whether training sees the converged prefix context that terminal KV sharing supplies at inference (Figure 3 a). A model trained at a single depth predicts best there but breaks KV sharing; Huginn’s fixed broad prior [ 2 ] supports sharing but dilutes supervision at the target depth more than sharing requires. We learn the prior from prediction feedback, which pulls supervision toward depths that predict well, and add an entropy term that keeps it broad enough for sharing. The second component is input injection [ 14 , 2 , 15 , 16 ] , which adds the input to the state at every recurrence. Huginn and Parcae leave the state’s component along the input unconstrained; depending on its sign, this component amplifies or cancels the injection. Our orthogonal input injection (OrthoInj) removes this component, so every recurrence receives the input at the same strength. • Fixed points explain the two existing shortcuts (Section 3 ): truncated backpropagation alone shapes the fixed points that terminal KV sharing relies on. Fixed-depth training with full backpropagation through time does not; at 1.6 1.6 B, sharing drops its GSM8K accuracy from 50.6 50.6 to 21.2 21.2 . With tolerant fixed points, sharing cuts the KV cache 3 × 3\times at five recurrences, keeping the entropy-regularized learned-prior models within 0.4 0.4 points of their full-cache downstream average. • Fixed points yield two new shortcuts. Distilled prefill (Section 5.5 ), trained on a quarter of the teacher’s pretraining tokens, is up to 1.79 × 1.79\times faster on 8 8 K prompts and trails the teacher’s downstream average by 1.0 1.0 – 4.5 4.5 points; at matched latency, it scores 0.5 0.5 – 0.9 0.9 points above the teacher prefilling with two recurrences. Rollout-state reuse (Section 3.1 ) halves the scoring and backward time of each RL update relative to replaying the loops with full backpropagation through time, and stays within 1.6 1.6 points of that baseline’s GSM8K pass@1. • The learned depth prior keeps prediction quality under terminal KV sharing (Section 5.2 ): from 100 100 M to 1.6 1.6 B, it lowers perplexity and raises the downstream average over Huginn’s fixed prior, and at 1.6 1.6 B, with a 3 × 3\times smaller KV cache, it even matches the full-cache downstream average of fixed-depth training. • OrthoInj improves on the strongest injection baseline, Parcae’s (Section 5.3 ). items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.06823 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Oct 2026] Title: Deep Learning for Sleep Heart Rate Estimation from Accelerometers: Toward Population-Scale Cardiac Insight Without Optical Sensors Authors: Tanbin Islam Rohan , Pranjol Sen Gupta , Tanusree Debi , Nazmus Sakib View a PDF of the paper titled Deep Learning for Sleep Heart Rate Estimation from Accelerometers: Toward Population-Scale Cardiac Insight Without Optical Sensors, by Tanbin Islam Rohan and 3 other authors View PDF Abstract: Large longitudinal cohorts often contain wrist accelerometry without optical heart-rate sensing, motivating recovery of cardiac information from motion signals already collected during sleep. We present SeqSmoother, a transformer-based temporal corrector for sleep heart rate (HR) estimation from wrist accelerometry. SeqSmoother combines spectral descriptors with an intermediate Nightbeat-derived frequency anchor and a physics-motivated sub-harmonic feature designed to identify harmonic frequency lock-on. All inference-time features are derived from wrist accelerometry, while ECG is used only to construct reference HR labels and training-label quality weights. We evaluate SeqSmoother using 13 participant-disjoint held-out folds and compare it with the official Nightbeat implementation under a matched 60-s window and 15-s step protocol. Across all out-of-fold predictions, SeqSmoother achieved a participant-macro MAE of 1.60 bpm. On Nightbeat-retained matched intervals, Nightbeat achieved lower absolute error than SeqSmoother (0.615 versus 1.091 bpm), while SeqSmoother provided estimates over a larger portion of the eligible recording; Nightbeat produced final estimates for 72.85% of the SeqSmoother-eligible out-of-fold grid. Separately, the proposed sub-harmonic ratio achieved an AUROC of 0.972 for identifying reference-defined harmonic lock-on candidates. These findings reveal an accuracy-availability trade-off between learned temporal modeling and quality-gated signal processing while providing empirical support for a physics-informed approach to identifying frequency-tracking failures in accelerometer-based sleep HR estimation. items.content: Computer Science > Machine Learning arXiv:2610.06822 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Oct 2026] Title: Private online learning and prediction for Littlestone classes Authors: Amartya Sanyal View a PDF of the paper titled Private online learning and prediction for Littlestone classes, by Amartya Sanyal View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We study mistake bounds for differentially private online learning and online prediction under oblivious realisable adversaries. Online learning requires the learner to release a hypothesis at each time step whereas in online prediction, the learner only needs to make predictions without releasing a hypothesis. Using a novel lower bound for private online learning and an upper bound for private prediction, we show that the sample complexity of these two problems are separated by a factor that grows with the time horizon for every class of finite Littlestone dimension $d$. First, we prove that every $\br{\epsilon,\delta}$-private online learner has a deterministic realisable stream of length $T$ on which the mistake bound is at least $\bE\bs{M_T}=\Om{\frac d\epsilon \log\br{ T}^{2/3}}$. In particular, this is the first non-trivial lower in the range $1/T<\delta<1/\log T)$ left open in earlier works[SR22,DSS24,LWY24]. Second, we prove that for every class of of Littlestone dimension $d$, there exists an $(\epsilon,\delta)$-jointly private predictor with at most $2^{2^{cd^2}}\epsilon^{-2}\log^2\br{2/\br{\epsilon\delta}}$ expected mistakes, independently of $T$, for some absolute constant $c>0$. Thus, for every fixed class of finite Littlestone dimension when $\delta=\Theta\br{1/\log T}$, private learning requires $\Om{\br{\log T}^{2/3}}$ expected mistakes, whereas private prediction admits $\bigO{\br{\log\log T}^2}$. It is well known that if the class ℋ {\mathcal{H}} has Littlestone dimension Ldim ⁡ ( ℋ ) = d \Ldim\left({{\mathcal{H}}}\right)=d , then the Standard Optimal Algorithm makes at most d d mistakes on any stream, independently of the horizon T T [ 11 ] . Additionally, this bound is also known to be tight; thus Littlestone dimension tightly characterises the mistake bound for realisable online learning. Whether this dependence on the horizon is necessary was posed as an open question in [ 13 ] . For POINT 3 \mathrm{POINT}_{3} , earlier work [ 5 ] used the concentration assumption that the learner with high probability predicts the same label at point 1 1 in an all-dummy stream. Then, the adversary inserts informative examples with the opposite label, which causes the learner to incur mistakes whenever it outputs its preferred label. Privacy constrains how these insertions change the output distribution. This allows the adversary to place informative examples where mistakes are likely. Our goal is to force mistakes without this concentration assumption. We instead sample a uniformly random bit B B at the beginning and use it as the label for every informative example. On the dummy stream, the prediction at point 1 1 is independent of B B , even if the predictions keep changing (i.e. no concentration or similar prior). For private prediction, we first construct a short private sequence of predictors that, with high probability, contains at least one with few mistakes on the full stream. The first difficulty is to bound the number of bad predictors in this list even when the hypothesis class is infinite. Using the idea of essential hypotheses [ 12 ] , we create multiple short lists of predictors with the useful property that predictors can be added to these lists online using only earlier mistakes. We then use a private selection mechanism to choose a frequently appearing predictor among these lists. A contradiction argument ( Lemma 3 ) then shows that the number of bad predictors is bounded independently of T T . The next challenge is to use these candidates privately online. Each candidate can be computed from the observed prefix once its predecessor has made enough mistakes. However, switching immediately to a new candidate can be privacy-violating. Unlike online learning, in online prediction, only the prediction at the current point is released. Thus, on dummy examples where the old and new predictors agree, the learner can switch its internal predictor while continuing to give the same answer that it would have given before the switch. We use a private replacement mechanism based on the Mirror mechanism [ 4 ] with increasing delays before each switch to implement this in a private manner. The key property is that, while the latest available candidate has made few mistakes, later candidates cannot change the current predictions. Since these mistakes are precisely what is needed to compute the next candidate, we can ignore that candidate until enough mistakes are made or for the rest of the game if this never happens. The resulting online predictor has a mistake bound Q Q , independent of T T , that holds with probability at least 1 − δ 1-\delta . We combine our predictor with a subsampled SOA algorithm [ 5 ] , whose expected mistakes are O ⁡ ( d / δ ) O\left(d/\delta\right) . Intuitively, this algorithm runs a competition between the two predictors and guarantees that the combined predictor competes with the better one in expectation, up to a constant factor and an additive term independent of T T ( Lemma 13 ). items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.06846 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Oct 2026] Title: BiasFlow: Geometric Monitoring and Backbone Regularization for Spurious Feature Reliance Authors: Haojin Deng , Zhiping Lin , Yimin Yang View a PDF of the paper titled BiasFlow: Geometric Monitoring and Backbone Regularization for Spurious Feature Reliance, by Haojin Deng and 2 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Worst-group accuracy (WGA) evaluates a trained predictor but does not characterize how its frozen backbone behaves when a new head is learned. We introduce BiasFlow, a hook-based toolkit for monitoring class-attribute centroid alignment (IBMI), within-class centroid separation (W-IBMI), and feature-projection sensitivity. IBMI is confounded by class-attribute correlation and is not a measure of causal feature reliance. We pair these diagnostics with BiasFlow Regularization (BFR), a supervised, composable class-conditional centroid-alignment penalty. W-IBMI verifies the quantity BFR optimizes; it is scale dependent and does not independently establish attribute removal. Across the reported small-scale benchmarks, adding BFR improves or preserves mean WGA, with gains up to +26.0 pp on UrbanCars. The principal independent stress test freezes CelebA-Std backbones and trains fresh heads on biased data: BFR+GroupDRO improves WGA from 40.7% to 64.1%, while Male probe accuracy decreases from 92.5% to 72.2%. Attribute information remains recoverable, and cross-task results are mixed. A controlled synthetic-watermark ImageNet experiment additionally improves watermark-shift accuracy by +23.0 pp under matched training. These results support evaluating centroid geometry and resistance to biased head retraining alongside WGA, within the tested protocols. Abstract Worst-group accuracy (WGA) evaluates a trained predictor but does not characterize how its frozen backbone behaves when a new head is learned. We introduce BiasFlow , a hook-based toolkit for monitoring class–attribute centroid alignment (IBMI), within-class centroid separation (W-IBMI), and feature-projection sensitivity. IBMI is confounded by class–attribute correlation and is not a measure of causal feature reliance. We pair these diagnostics with BiasFlow Regularization (BFR) , a supervised, composable class-conditional centroid-alignment penalty. W-IBMI verifies the quantity BFR optimizes; it is scale dependent and does not independently establish attribute removal. Across the reported small-scale benchmarks, adding BFR improves or preserves mean WGA, with gains up to + 26.0 +26.0 pp on UrbanCars. The principal independent stress test freezes CelebA-Std backbones and trains fresh heads on biased data: BFR+GroupDRO improves WGA from 40.7 % 40.7\% to 64.1 % 64.1\% , while Male probe accuracy decreases from 92.5 % 92.5\% to 72.2 % 72.2\% . Attribute information remains recoverable, and cross-task results are mixed. A controlled synthetic-watermark ImageNet experiment additionally improves watermark-shift accuracy by + 23.0 +23.0 pp under matched training. These results support evaluating centroid geometry and resistance to biased head retraining alongside WGA, within the tested protocols. Index Terms: Spurious correlations, debiasing, representation learning, geometric probing, worst-group accuracy, backbone regularization, feature space analysis, deep learning. I Introduction Spurious correlations can arise when a target label co-occurs with a task-irrelevant attribute in the training data. Empirical Risk Minimization (ERM) may exploit such correlations and fail when they change [ 1 ] . This problem occurs in facial attribute recognition [ 2 ] and visual group-shift benchmarks [ 3 ] . Fig. 1: t-SNE of CelebA-Std ResNet-18 features, seed 1 (Blond Hair target, Male attribute). Baseline and BFR panels illustrate different within-class subgroup layouts. BFR reduces the targeted centroid discrepancy; two-dimensional mixing does not establish concept erasure or causal feature use. Over the past several years, the community has developed a rich family of debiasing methods aimed at minimizing spurious reliance while preserving overall model performance. Loss-reweighting strategies such as LfF [ 4 ] and JTT [ 5 ] , head-retraining approaches such as DFR [ 6 ] , adversarial discoverers such as DebiAN [ 7 ] , and group-robust optimizers such as GroupDRO [ 3 ] have all reported substantial improvements on the standard evaluation benchmark: Worst-Group Accuracy (WGA), the minimum accuracy over evaluated groups defined by the cross-product of class and spurious attribute. WGA is the minimum accuracy over predefined evaluation groups; it does not summarize confidence margins, representation geometry, or the behavior of a subsequently trained classifier. Models with different representations can have the same WGA. DFR [ 6 ] demonstrates that a group-balanced head can improve WGA while its input backbone is held fixed. This is a useful strategy, not evidence that the original classifier necessarily uses every attribute encoded by its backbone. We ask the narrower question of whether a frozen representation remains susceptible to a new head trained under the original biased distribution, consistent with the distinction between representation and classifier studied in [ 8 , 1 ] . We introduce BiasFlow to inspect this distinction through geometric measurements and head-retraining stress tests. The Inter-class Bias-alignment Metric Index (IBMI) measures centroid alignment with a pooled, user-specified attribute direction. Because class composition contributes to that direction, a high IBMI can occur even without within-class attribute separation. We therefore interpret IBMI as an observational summary, not proof of reliance or contamination. DFR preserves its own first-stage backbone during head retraining; equality with a separately trained ERM run requires identical checkpoint and probe conditions, which the audit does not enforce. The projection probe defines signed group accuracy changes, but the retained figure plots unsigned AblGap. Its nonnegative bars establish neither exploitation nor interference. The independent stress test is particularly informative on CelebA-Std 1 1 1 CelebA-Std uses Blond Hair as target and Male as the spurious attribute, with the Blond-Male group rare [ 3 ] . . GroupDRO achieves 86.3 % 86.3\% end-to-end WGA, but a fresh head trained on the standard biased data over its frozen backbone obtains 40.7 % 40.7\% , close to ERM’s 40.0 % 40.0\% (Table IX ). Male probe accuracy is 92.5 % 92.5\% . These are distinct observations: a new biased head performs poorly, and a separate probe can recover the attribute. Neither establishes that GroupDRO’s original head uses Male causally. Our intervention is deliberately restricted to the first moments of class-conditional attribute groups. BiasFlow Regularization (BFR) penalizes the distance between their feature centroids during backbone training. It belongs to the established family of conditional representation-alignment methods [ 9 , 10 , 11 ] ; its role here is a simple composable intervention paired with geometric monitoring and a frozen-backbone evaluation. Equal centroids do not imply equal feature distributions or attribute erasure. BFR reduces the objective-aligned W-IBMI statistic in most configurations (Table IV ). More independently, BFR+GroupDRO yields 64.1 % 64.1\% biased-head WGA and 72.2 % 72.2\% Male probe accuracy, compared with 40.7 % 40.7\% and 92.5 % 92.5\% without BFR. The former tests resistance to biased head retraining; the latter measures recoverability under the specified probe. Figure 1 illustrates within-class subgroup mixing in a two-dimensional visualization, which should not be interpreted as proof of complete distribution alignment. Our contributions are summarized as follows: • Geometric monitoring with explicit scope. BiasFlow reports pooled centroid alignment, class-conditional centroid separation, and projection sensitivity. We specify class-composition and scale limitations, and distinguish the unsigned AblGap from signed group accuracy drops. These summaries complement WGA; they do not certify fairness, causal reliance, or concept removal. • Composable supervised centroid regularization. BFR applies class-conditional centroid alignment to the evaluated training objectives. We retain the reported WGA results, including the near-neutral Waterbirds JTT case, and distinguish supervised comparisons from gains over methods without training-time attribute labels. We do not claim that conditional alignment itself is new or that BFR outperforms unevaluated representation-level methods. • Frozen-backbone stress testing. Fresh biased heads on CelebA-Std provide the primary independent evidence: GroupDRO’s backbone supports 40.7 % 40.7\% WGA, versus 64.1 % 64.1\% for BFR+GroupDRO. Appendix experiments report continued ERM training, Smiling transfer, and alternative attribute probes, including negative outcomes. A separate controlled synthetic-watermark study tests a large-scale nuisance intervention under matched training. II Related Work Spurious-correlation mitigation includes predictive-loss methods, head retraining, and a substantial literature on representation alignment, adversarial removal, and concept erasure. We discuss these families to position BFR as a centroid-level instance of representation regularization rather than the first representation-level intervention. II-A Predictive-Loss and Head-Retraining Methods The baselines evaluated here span sample reweighting, head retraining, and group-supervised robust optimization. Reweighting and group-loss training can change the entire network, including the backbone; only the head-retraining stage of DFR explicitly leaves the backbone fixed. Loss-Reweighting Approaches. These methods aim to improve Worst-Group Accuracy (WGA) by dynamically altering the importance of training samples without requiring explicit group annotations. Just Train Twice (JTT) [ 5 ] identifies misclassified samples from a standard ERM model and upweights them in a second training phase. Learning from Failure (LfF) [ 4 ] simultaneously trains a biased network to amplify prejudice and a debiased network that focuses on samples the biased model struggles with. Similarly, Debiasing Alternate Networks (DebiAN) [ 7 ] employs an adversarial setup to discover and unlearn unknown biases. These methods can shift the final decision rule toward minority or shortcut-conflicting samples, but they regulate training through sample weights rather than explicit representation constraints. Consequently, the backbone remains free to encode spurious attributes even when the output classifier becomes more robust. Classification Head Retraining. DFR [ 6 ] retrains a linear head on balanced data over a frozen ERM-trained backbone. It demonstrates that useful core features can already be present. Our stress test concerns a later biased head, not a defect in the balanced DFR decision rule. Head retraining preserves an existing representation and can avoid the cost of relearning it. BFR instead changes the backbone during its training stage. These interventions answer different questions: robust prediction with a selected head, versus the behavior of new heads on frozen features. Neither approach universally dominates, particularly when transferred tasks benefit from the targeted attribute. Debiasing with Explicit Bias Annotations. When spurious group labels are available, methods can directly enforce robustness. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) [ 12 ] seeks representations that support invariant prediction across training environments, offering a theoretical route to avoiding environment-specific shortcuts. Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GroupDRO) [ 3 ] minimizes the maximum loss across predefined groups. Recent advancements have extended this paradigm: Hierarchical Group DRO [ 13 ] addresses both inter-group and intra-group distributional shifts through a multi-level ambiguity set, while LISA (Learning Invariant Predictors with Selective Augmentation) [ 14 ] leverages group labels to perform selective mixup interpolation, effectively canceling out spurious correlations during training. These methods enforce outcome robustness through group-level losses or augmentations, but high WGA does not by itself certify that the backbone has become invariant to the spurious attribute. II-B Latent and Causal Fairness Metrics To look beyond output accuracy, recent work has developed metrics to quantify bias directly within learned features. Observational Probes. Information-theoretic approaches measure statistical dependence. For instance, InfoFair [ 15 ] minimizes variational mutual information between outcomes and sensitive attributes, while Gowri et al. [ 16 ] propose scalable approximations for high-dimensional latent mutual information. Geometrically, Zhou et al. [ 17 ] introduce Fair CCA to minimize correlation disparity across groups via canonical correlations, and Frolov and Oseledets [ 18 ] use principal angle alignments to quantify subspace relationships. These metrics expose structure that output accuracy cannot see, but they are generally not designed as lightweight monitoring tools for debiasing pipelines or tied to a corresponding backbone-level training objective. Interventional Probing. Interventional metrics test whether representations actively influence predictions rather than merely encoding information. Guerner et al. [ 19 ] perform feature-space interventions on learned subspaces to verify if specific concepts drive model predictions, offering stronger evidence of debiasing than observational correlation. However, such probes are usually used as post-hoc analyses; they rarely distinguish whether a spurious feature is being exploited as a shortcut or acting as interference, and they do not prescribe how to reshape the backbone. II-C Relationship to Prior Work Conditional alignment is established prior work. Conditional Learning of Fair Representations [ 9 ] aligns representations across demographic groups conditional on class to address equalized error rates. Correct-N-Contrast (CNC) [ 10 ] uses an ERM model to identify same-class examples with different spurious cues and learns aligned representations contrastively without training-time attribute labels; it also connects alignment to worst-group error. BFR uses supplied attribute labels and a first-moment penalty, so it offers neither CNC’s annotation advantage nor full conditional distribution matching. Learning Not to Learn [ 20 ] adversarially suppresses bias information through a feature–bias mutual-information objective. EnD [ 21 ] regularizes intermediate representations by entangling same-target features and disentangling bias-related features. LEACE [ 22 ] performs closed-form linear concept erasure with guarantees for the transformed representation; BFR’s approximate conditional centroid alignment has no comparable erasure guarantee. Spurious Correlation-Aware Embedding Regularization (SCER) [ 11 ] derives core and spurious directions from group-wise mean embeddings and regularizes the embedding space for worst-group robustness. SCER is especially close in its use of group means, while its direction- and classifier-based theoretical motivation differs from BFR’s direct within-class centroid penalty. Our contribution is the monitoring and evaluation workflow around a composable penalty. The experiments do not include these close representation-level baselines and cannot establish superiority over them. When spurious group labels are available, methods can directly enforce robustness. Invariant Risk Minimization (IRM) [ 12 ] seeks representations that support invariant prediction across training environments, offering a theoretical route to avoiding environment-specific shortcuts. Group Distributionally Robust Optimization (GroupDRO) [ 3 ] minimizes the maximum loss across predefined groups. Conditional Learning of Fair Representations [ 9 ] aligns representations across demographic groups conditional on class to address equalized error rates. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.06824 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Oct 2026] Title: TasteVal: Measuring the Experimental Research Taste of AI Systems Against Human Experts Authors: Oliver Jaffe , Dane Sherburn View a PDF of the paper titled TasteVal: Measuring the Experimental Research Taste of AI Systems Against Human Experts, by Oliver Jaffe and 1 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: We introduce TasteVal, a benchmark to evaluate the experimental research taste of frontier models. We define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results. TasteVal measures the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes. We operationalize experimental research taste as compute efficiency; a Researcher who reaches the same score as an expert human using half the serial experimental compute has twice the experimental taste. Experimental taste thus acts as a multiplier on experimental compute, making it a key input to forecasts of AI progress. TasteVal consists of 8 novel, challenging, open-ended tasks representative of frontier AI R&D. To isolate taste from coding ability, the model under evaluation acts as a Researcher that iteratively designs experiments while a fixed Coder agent implements them and reports their results. The Researcher executes until either the 40 H100 hour or 120 wall-clock hour budgets are exhausted. We recruit 24 human experts, at least 2 per task, and take the best expert attempt per task as the expert baseline. We evaluate 20 models released between 2023 and 2026. The best-performing model, Opus 5.5, exceeds our expert baseline, with a compute multiplier of 2.3x (95% CI 1.15-4.37), at roughly 1/30 of our baseliners' average per-run cost. On TasteVal, the compute multiplier of frontier models has doubled approximately every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7-5.0), up from every 14 months between 2023 and December 2025. Measured by final normalized performance, frontier models show no trend break, doubling every 14.6 months. To keep TasteVal uncontaminated, we do not release the tasks.
