items.content: TasteVal: Measuring the Experimental Research Taste of AI Systems Against Human Experts Oliver Jaffe † † thanks: Corresponding author: ollie@pzeroresearch.com Dane Sherburn Affiliation: P-Zero Research Abstract We introduce TasteVal, a benchmark to evaluate the experimental research taste of frontier models. We define research taste as the ability to pick interesting problems to solve, design experiments, and interpret experimental results. TasteVal measures the experimental component of research taste; given a fixed research problem, we measure how well a model iteratively designs experiments and draws conclusions from their outcomes. We operationalize experimental research taste as compute efficiency; a Researcher who reaches the same score as an expert human using half the serial experimental compute has twice the experimental taste. Experimental taste thus acts as a multiplier on experimental compute, making it a key input to forecasts of AI progress. TasteVal consists of 8 novel, challenging, open-ended tasks representative of frontier AI R&D. To isolate taste from coding ability, the model under evaluation acts as a Researcher that iteratively designs experiments while a fixed Coder agent implements them and reports their results. The Researcher executes until either the 40 H100 hour or 120 wall-clock hour budgets are exhausted. We recruit 24 human experts, at least 2 per task, and take the best expert attempt per task as the expert baseline. We evaluate 20 models released between 2023 and 2026. The best-performing model, Opus 5.5, exceeds our expert baseline, with a compute multiplier of 2.3x (95% CI 1.15–4.37), at roughly 1/30 of our baseliners’ average per-run cost. On TasteVal, the compute multiplier of frontier models has doubled approximately every 3.0 months since December 2025 (95% CI 1.7–5.0), up from every 14 months between 2023 and December 2025. Measured by normalized final performance, frontier models show no trend break, doubling every 14.6 months. To keep TasteVal uncontaminated, we do not release the tasks. 1 Introduction AI agents are increasingly capable of automating AI R&D. Agents now approach the cost-effectiveness of expert researchers on frontier-adjacent optimization tasks ( Cunningham et al., 2026b ) , and are reported to be automating a large amount of AI R&D inside frontier labs ( Anthropic, 2026a ; OpenAI, 2026 ) . Frontier safety frameworks consider automated AI R&D an important capability to track ( OpenAI, 2025 ; Anthropic, 2026b ; Google DeepMind, 2026 ) , and forecasts of when superhuman AI capabilities will arrive depend heavily on estimates of how quickly AI R&D automation is advancing ( Kokotajlo et al., 2025 ) . In particular, several takeoff models examine a “software-only intelligence explosion” in which AI-driven improvements to AI software become self-sustaining and capabilities advance rapidly even with fixed physical compute ( Davidson and Eth, 2025 ) . Figure 1: The compute multiplier of models has doubled every 3.0 months (95% CI 1.7–5.0 months) since December 2025, up from every 14.0 months before. Each point is one model’s compute multiplier relative to our expert baseline (1x), plotted against its release date. At-the-time frontier models are shown in dark green and used for the fits; non-frontier models are shown in light green. The dashed lines are separate log-linear fits before and after the break at the release of GPT-5.2 ( R 2 = 0.96 R^{2}=0.96 ), and the shaded regions their 95% bands. Error bars are 95% intervals from a two-level hierarchical bootstrap with 1,000 resamples, drawing first over tasks and then over runs within each task. Two broad capabilities drive progress in AI R&D. The first is implementation : writing code, debugging, and running experiments. The second is research taste : deciding what problems are worth solving, what experiments are worth running, and what to conclude from experimental results ( Huang, 2026 ) . Implementation capabilities are extensively covered by software engineering evaluations and machine learning engineering evaluations. However, to our knowledge no benchmark measures research taste prospectively (before the outcome of the chosen experiment is known) against realized outcomes, in isolation from implementation. End-to-end benchmarks are prospective but entangle taste with implementation ( Chan et al., 2024 ; Wijk et al., 2024 ) . Most dedicated evaluations of research judgment are retrospective, either by ranking completed papers ( Mahajan et al., 2025 ; Tong et al., 2026 ; Ye et al., 2026 ) or by matching generated ideas to later high-impact papers ( Jiang, 2026 ) . TASTE ( Baig et al., 2026 ) is prospective and isolates judgment, but scores against expert preferences rather than realized outcomes. We introduce TasteVal, a benchmark that directly measures the experimental component of research taste: given a research problem, we evaluate how well a model designs experiments and interprets their results. TasteVal consists of 8 uncontaminated AI R&D tasks created from scratch spanning curating pre-training data, pre-training language models, fine-tuning pre-trained models, modeling human preferences, aligning models against adversarial prompts, and more. We also design tasks to resist saturation, so that models that far exceed our expert baseline performance can still be evaluated. Serial and parallel compute are not interchangeable, since a longer run allows more rounds of learning from results, while a bigger cluster only allows more experiments per round. Two runs rarely end at the same score, so we compare them at the weaker run’s endpoint score: the test score of the official submission. The stronger run’s compute is the GPU hours at which it first reached that score, and the weaker run’s compute is its whole compute budget ( Figure 3 ). A run’s curve is the test score of its selected submission over time. Until the run produces the submission it will later mark official, the selected submission is its best on validation so far; from then on it is the official submission. We calculate the compute multiplier per run as the expert baseline’s compute divided by the model’s compute at the weaker run’s endpoint score. We compute a model’s compute multiplier as the geometric mean of its run multipliers over seeds within each task, then over tasks. Figure 3: Computing the compute multiplier and the performance multiplier for a single run. Each curve shows the normalized score (naive baseline 0, expert baseline 1) of the run’s selected submission as a function of GPU hours spent: its best on validation so far, until it produces the submission it will mark official. Because two runs rarely end at the same score, we compare them at the weaker run’s endpoint score (here the human’s). The stronger run’s compute is the GPU hours at which it first reached that score (20 hours for the model), and the weaker run’s compute is its whole budget (40 hours). This gives a compute multiplier of 40 / 20 = 2 40/20=2 x: the model reached the expert’s final score with half the compute. The performance multiplier is the ratio of the runs’ final normalized scores, regardless of compute: the model ends at 1.5 and the expert at 1, so the model’s performance multiplier is 1.5x. However, this compares a model directly with the expert baseline, which only works for models near human level. Every run whose official test score falls below the score of the expert baseline’s first submission gets the same multiplier on that task so the metric cannot rank models below that point. Similarly, a model that exceeds the baseline’s best score has its multiplier set by how quickly it reached that score, so how far beyond it the model performs does not change its multiplier. To mitigate this, we use three references (GPT-4, Opus 5.0 (max), and the expert baseline), and compare each model with the reference closest to it in release date, defining the “release date” of the expert baseline as the release date of Opus 4.8. This gives an older model (such as GPT-4o) a multiplier in GPT-4 units, and a frontier model (such as Fable 5.1) a multiplier in Opus 5.0 units. To put them into human-baseline units, we multiply the ratios of compute multipliers between neighboring references in order to convert a model’s multiplier into human-baseline units. See Appendix H.1 for the full explanation of the metric. 2.5.2 Performance Multiplier The performance multiplier measures how good a Researcher’s final result is relative to the expert baseline, regardless of how much compute it took to get there. A run’s performance multiplier is the test score of the run’s official submission, rescaled so that the naive baseline scores 0 and the expert baseline’s score on that task (the official test score) scores 1. For example, a run that matches the expert baseline’s score has a performance multiplier of 1x, and a run halfway between the naive baseline and the expert baseline has 0.5x. items.content: \workshoptitle AI for Chip Design Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification Je Yang † † thanks: Work done while interning at Google. Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Columbia University Affiliation: New York, NY, USA Email: je.yang@cs.columbia.edu Ivan Lobov Affiliation: Google DeepMind Affiliation: London, United Kingdom Email: lobov@google.com Thomas Karpati Affiliation: Google Affiliation: Mountain View, CA, USA Email: tkarpati@google.com Abstract The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip—yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future ( BTTF ) , an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification. 1 Introduction Sustaining the computational demands of modern AI beyond the end of Moore’s law increasingly hinges on highly heterogeneous Systems-on-Chip (SoCs) Yang et al. (2026) . As architectural complexity grows, design flows built on Hardware Description Languages (HDLs) become ever more labor-intensive, iterative, and error-prone Hu et al. (2025) . Verification alone now consumes over 70% of the development cycle becoming the primary bottleneck of modern chip design Cadence Design Systems (2024) , and functional bugs that slip into full-chip regression or post-silicon testing carry exponential financial and schedule penalties. Hence, automating register-transfer level (RTL) verification and analysis is an urgent, high-impact goal for the Electronic Design Automation (EDA) community. The rapid advances of Large Language Models (LLMs) has naturally inspired a wave of AI-assisted EDA research Kang et al. (2025) ; Ping et al. (2026) . This wave, however, is strikingly lopsided. While approximately 74.6% of LLM-for-hardware studies concentrate on front-end RTL code generation and synthesis Abdollahi et al. (2024) , post-simulation waveform debugging and dynamic verification remain largely underexplored. Since hardware development demands rigorous testing as much as design synthesis, this neglect leaves a substantial share of the automation opportunity untapped. Even the few LLM-aided verification workflows that do exist operate almost exclusively on static source code or toy-scale simulation logs, whereas interactive post-simulation debugging is a fundamentally harder problem. When a dynamic simulation fails, engineers manually scrub through terabytes of temporal dumps in graphical waveform viewers, tracing illegal transitions back to their origin in the HDL hierarchy. Frontier LLM agents are locked out of this loop by what we term Infrastructural Impedance . Raw, ASCII-based waveform dumps exceed model context windows by orders of magnitude, carry no structured semantic index, and expose no native, low-latency query interface that an autonomous agent could invoke. Here, we propose Back-to-the-Future ( BTTF ) , an end-to-end agentic framework that enables natural-language querying for root-cause analysis and formal verification over complex RTL waveforms. Rather than forcing waveforms into an LLM’s context, BTTF revisits a classical EDA paradigm. It recasts unstructured temporal waveforms as a normalized relational SQLite database, then pairs this schema with a collaborative multi-agent engine that plans, queries, and audits on the engineer’s behalf. On 150 expert-annotated queries, BTTF reaches 95.33% overall accuracy, and its multi-agent design outscores a monolithic single-agent baseline by 17.3% on a five-criteria quality audit. 2 Related Work LLM-Driven Hardware Verification. LLMs have demonstrated remarkable capacity across EDA research, assisting developers with bug localization, code generation, and automated verification Hu et al. (2025) ; Kang et al. (2025) ; Ping et al. (2026) ; Zhao et al. (2025) ; Mastropaolo et al. (2023) ; Alvanaki et al. (2026) . For complex verification tasks, state-of-the-art systems increasingly adopt multi-agent orchestration flows that split hardware synthesis into specialized roles for generation, testbench simulation, and formal counterexample refinement Ping et al. (2026) ; Zhao et al. (2025) ; Pan et al. (2026) . Yet these frameworks operate predominantly on static source code, compile-time assertion lists, or toy-scale simulation logs, implicitly assuming an LLM can localize functional errors from static HDL traces or terse compiler messages alone. Key Limitation and Our Observation. The closest attempt to bridge this gap equips a coding agent with an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-based waveform tracing tool Ho et al. (2025) , but such traces remain tied to small, code-centric examples rather than production dumps. BTTF instead builds on a complementary observation: SQL generation is an emergent capability of LLMs, rooted in their deep semantic mapping from natural language to structured code Gao et al. (2023) . Once waveforms are made relational , decades of database machinery (e.g., indexing, aggregation, low-latency filtering) become directly accessible to language agents. 3 BTTF Framework Figure 1: Overview of BTTF framework. As Figure 1 illustrates, BTTF comprises two coupled subsystems on opposite sides of a single relational contract: (1) an offline Waveform Preprocessing Pipeline that compresses bulky simulation dumps into an optimized relational SQLite schema, and (2) an online Agentic Orchestration Engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL and carries out the verification itself. 3.1 Waveform Preprocessing Pipeline Standard EDA simulators emit proprietary binary waveforms ( .fsdb ) or ASCII Value Change Dump ( .vcd ) files; for SoC-scale blocks, a raw VCD text file routinely exceeds 10 GB—far beyond any prospect of direct context embedding. The BTTF pipeline therefore extracts the target hierarchies and normalizes them into a relational SQLite database ( waves.db ) built around two primary tables: • signal_metadata captures the static signal declarations (RTL signal name and its variable type, etc.) with id. • signal_changes records the temporal behavior as timestamped transitions as a (time, value) with a foreign key to refer metadata. Separating who a signal is from what it does lets agents reason over structure and time independently, joining the two only when a query demands it. A naïve translation of every value change would simply move the scalability problem from the filesystem into the database. BTTF instead applies coverage-aware pruning during on-the-fly database generation: • Clock pruning . High-frequency clock toggles dominate table size while carrying little debug information; since every row in signal_changes is timestamped, clock transitions can be skipped at insertion time without losing temporal anchoring. • On-the-fly inactive-signal pruning ( zero / avg ). To cope with duplicate VCD identifiers and inactive nets, the ingestion engine maintains a lightweight hash map ( vcd_id_to_db_id ) alongside a per-signal transition counter ( signal_change_count ). This bookkeeping enables two graduated policies: dropping statically silent zero-toggle wires ( zero ), or additionally dropping nets whose toggle rate falls below the design-wide average ( avg ). • Batched insertion. Row-by-row insertion incurs severe SQLite transaction overhead. Grouping transitions into batched writes removes this bottleneck at ingestion time. 3.2 LLM-Driven Agent Orchestration On top of the generated waves.db , BTTF conducts verification through a collaborative multi-agent architecture. The main Orchestration Agent decomposes a natural-language query into sub-goals, routes them to specialized agents with own toolsets, and audits the merged answer. • Analysis Agent. Armed with schema-aware multi-query execution tools, it composes SQLite queries over the two tables to handle scope discovery, event inspection, and toggle counting. For complex tasks such as power hotspot detection, it leverages an iterative function-calling loop to execute multi-turn queries and aggregate multi-cycle signal statistics. • Verification Agent. Tying waveform anomalies back to version-controlled source by evaluating SVA rules ( ASSERT , ASSERT_STATIC , ASSERT_NEVER , ASSERT_KNOWN , COVER ) through the regular expression (REGEX) assignment. • Evaluation Agent. Before any root-cause analysis is returned, this agent audits candidate queries against five criteria: (1) correctness —filtering, aggregation, and join fidelity to user intent; (2) completeness —inclusion of all required columns and time conditions; (3) efficiency —proper indexing and avoidance of redundant joins; (4) schema adherence —strict conformance to the two-table schema; and (5) context understanding —correct inference of implicit simulation timescales and hierarchy scopes. Under the orchestrator, agents communicate solely through a dynamic session context maintained across turns; together with a self-correction loop on failed queries, this shared-memory discipline lets each agent stay narrowly specialized without losing global coherence. Furthermore, when an assertion rule is violated even after self-correction, the agent autonomously isolates the exact violation timestamp and pinpoints the problematic sub-signals responsible for the failure (see Appendix A.1 for detailed root-cause diagnostics). 4 Results Experimental setup. All agents are served through the Gemini API with Gemini-2.5-Pro as the default model. Our benchmark spans multiple SoC design hierarchies of varying complexity (4.2 GB of VCD, 18,450 nets), from which we extract simulation windows ranging from narrow 50 ns high-resolution glitch-debug windows to 800 ns full-transaction simulation dumps. We curate 150 natural-language verification queries representative of daily engineering workflows, each paired with an expert-annotated golden answer. Preprocessing Performance. Pruning Strategy Footprint Reduc. Latency Coverage Fully Unpruned 1,420 MB 0.00% 410.5 ms 100.00% Clock Removed 480 MB 66.20% 125.2 ms 98.51% Zero-Toggle Pruned 395 MB 72.18% 94.8 ms 100.00% Below-Avg Pruned 185 MB 86.97% 41.6 ms 64.23% Table 1: Trade-off of waveform preprocessing across pruning strategies. Batch 1 Batch 10 Batch 50 Batch 100 0 0 100 100 200 200 240.5 240.5 100.2 100.2 85.4 85.4 83.2 83.2 Time (s) Figure 2: DB generation time speedup with batch insertion. We first quantify the cost of turning a waveform into an agent-ready database. As Table 1 shows, suppressing clock insertion alone shrinks the footprint by 66.20% and cuts query latency by 3.28 × 3.28\times while preserving 98.51% of functional toggle coverage. Additionally pruning untoggled signals pushes the reduction to 72.18%, while retaining full coverage over active nets. Aggressive below-average pruning compresses furthest but sacrifices 35.77% of coverage, marking the boundary of safe reduction. Relational schema optimization is thus not an implementation detail but a prerequisite for responsive agent interaction. Figure 2 confirms ingestion-side scalability. Batched insertion via SQL EXECUTEMANY accelerates database generation by up to 2.89 × 2.89\times over single-row insertion, removing the I/O bottleneck for multi-terabyte waveforms. BTTF Framework Performance. Table 2: Comprehensive taxonomy of verification tasks, example natural language user queries, and proof-of-concept execution accuracy. Domain Task / Query Type Example Natural Language Query Accuracy Debugging Scope/Net Discovery “List all logics in the moduleA .” 100.00% RTL Attribution “Find the RTL file related to logicA .” 87.50% Value Inspection “What is the value of logicA at time timeA ?” 95.00% Value Change Count “How many times has logicA changed?” 100.00% Event Timing Check “When is net logicA first set to valueA ?” 100.00% Analyzing Toggle Coverage “Calculate overall toggle coverage in jobA.db .” 91.67% Power Hotspot “Give me the 100ns window with max signal activities.” 91.67% Verification Static SVA Check “Verify ASSERT_STATIC(...) .” 84.62% Dynamic SVA Check “Run rule ASSERT_KNOWN(...) .” 90.91% Table 2 summarizes BTTF ’s coverage across routine debugging, toggle-based performance analysis, and formal verification. Over the full 150-query taxonomy, BTTF achieves 95.33% overall accuracy—near-perfect on debugging primitives and consistently reliable on the harder analysis and verification tasks. A detailed breakdown of representative verification queries, agent tool invocations, and synthesized output responses across all task categories is provided in Appendix A.2 (Table 3 ). We further compare a monolithic single-agent design against our collaborative architecture, with an autorater judging outputs on the Evaluation Agent’s five criteria. items.raw_text: \workshoptitle AI for Chip Design Back to the Future: Rethinking EDA Infrastructure for Agentic Systems in Chip Design Verification Je Yang † † thanks: Work done while interning at Google. Affiliation: Department of Computer Science Affiliation: Columbia University Affiliation: New York, NY, USA Email: je.yang@cs.columbia.edu Ivan Lobov Affiliation: Google DeepMind Affiliation: London, United Kingdom Email: lobov@google.com Thomas Karpati Affiliation: Google Affiliation: Mountain View, CA, USA Email: tkarpati@google.com Abstract The unprecedented computational scale of modern artificial intelligence depends on complex, multi-billion-transistor Systems-on-Chip—yet the workflows that verify these chips remain stubbornly manual. Although Large Language Models (LLMs) have made rapid inroads into Electronic Design Automation (EDA), approximately 74.6% of existing studies target static Register-Transfer Level (RTL) code generation, leaving post-simulation verification and interactive waveform debugging largely untouched. We introduce Back-to-the-Future ( BTTF ) , an end-to-end agentic framework that closes this infrastructural gap. BTTF distills massive, unstructured simulation dumps into a normalized relational SQLite database and couples it with a collaborative multi-agent orchestration engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL while correlating signal anomalies with versioned RTL repositories. Across a 150-query benchmark, BTTF attains 95.33% execution accuracy, charting a practical path toward autonomous EDA verification. 1 Introduction Sustaining the computational demands of modern AI beyond the end of Moore’s law increasingly hinges on highly heterogeneous Systems-on-Chip (SoCs) Yang et al. (2026) . As architectural complexity grows, design flows built on Hardware Description Languages (HDLs) become ever more labor-intensive, iterative, and error-prone Hu et al. (2025) . Verification alone now consumes over 70% of the development cycle becoming the primary bottleneck of modern chip design Cadence Design Systems (2024) , and functional bugs that slip into full-chip regression or post-silicon testing carry exponential financial and schedule penalties. Hence, automating register-transfer level (RTL) verification and analysis is an urgent, high-impact goal for the Electronic Design Automation (EDA) community. The rapid advances of Large Language Models (LLMs) has naturally inspired a wave of AI-assisted EDA research Kang et al. (2025) ; Ping et al. (2026) . This wave, however, is strikingly lopsided. While approximately 74.6% of LLM-for-hardware studies concentrate on front-end RTL code generation and synthesis Abdollahi et al. (2024) , post-simulation waveform debugging and dynamic verification remain largely underexplored. Since hardware development demands rigorous testing as much as design synthesis, this neglect leaves a substantial share of the automation opportunity untapped. Even the few LLM-aided verification workflows that do exist operate almost exclusively on static source code or toy-scale simulation logs, whereas interactive post-simulation debugging is a fundamentally harder problem. When a dynamic simulation fails, engineers manually scrub through terabytes of temporal dumps in graphical waveform viewers, tracing illegal transitions back to their origin in the HDL hierarchy. Frontier LLM agents are locked out of this loop by what we term Infrastructural Impedance . Raw, ASCII-based waveform dumps exceed model context windows by orders of magnitude, carry no structured semantic index, and expose no native, low-latency query interface that an autonomous agent could invoke. Here, we propose Back-to-the-Future ( BTTF ) , an end-to-end agentic framework that enables natural-language querying for root-cause analysis and formal verification over complex RTL waveforms. Rather than forcing waveforms into an LLM’s context, BTTF revisits a classical EDA paradigm. It recasts unstructured temporal waveforms as a normalized relational SQLite database, then pairs this schema with a collaborative multi-agent engine that plans, queries, and audits on the engineer’s behalf. On 150 expert-annotated queries, BTTF reaches 95.33% overall accuracy, and its multi-agent design outscores a monolithic single-agent baseline by 17.3% on a five-criteria quality audit. 2 Related Work LLM-Driven Hardware Verification. LLMs have demonstrated remarkable capacity across EDA research, assisting developers with bug localization, code generation, and automated verification Hu et al. (2025) ; Kang et al. (2025) ; Ping et al. (2026) ; Zhao et al. (2025) ; Mastropaolo et al. (2023) ; Alvanaki et al. (2026) . For complex verification tasks, state-of-the-art systems increasingly adopt multi-agent orchestration flows that split hardware synthesis into specialized roles for generation, testbench simulation, and formal counterexample refinement Ping et al. (2026) ; Zhao et al. (2025) ; Pan et al. (2026) . Yet these frameworks operate predominantly on static source code, compile-time assertion lists, or toy-scale simulation logs, implicitly assuming an LLM can localize functional errors from static HDL traces or terse compiler messages alone. Key Limitation and Our Observation. The closest attempt to bridge this gap equips a coding agent with an Abstract Syntax Tree (AST)-based waveform tracing tool Ho et al. (2025) , but such traces remain tied to small, code-centric examples rather than production dumps. BTTF instead builds on a complementary observation: SQL generation is an emergent capability of LLMs, rooted in their deep semantic mapping from natural language to structured code Gao et al. (2023) . Once waveforms are made relational , decades of database machinery (e.g., indexing, aggregation, low-latency filtering) become directly accessible to language agents. 3 BTTF Framework Figure 1: Overview of BTTF framework. As Figure 1 illustrates, BTTF comprises two coupled subsystems on opposite sides of a single relational contract: (1) an offline Waveform Preprocessing Pipeline that compresses bulky simulation dumps into an optimized relational SQLite schema, and (2) an online Agentic Orchestration Engine that translates natural-language verification queries into schema-aware SQL and carries out the verification itself. 3.1 Waveform Preprocessing Pipeline Standard EDA simulators emit proprietary binary waveforms ( .fsdb ) or ASCII Value Change Dump ( .vcd ) files; for SoC-scale blocks, a raw VCD text file routinely exceeds 10 GB—far beyond any prospect of direct context embedding. The BTTF pipeline therefore extracts the target hierarchies and normalizes them into a relational SQLite database ( waves.db ) built around two primary tables: • signal_metadata captures the static signal declarations (RTL signal name and its variable type, etc.) with id. • signal_changes records the temporal behavior as timestamped transitions as a (time, value) with a foreign key to refer metadata. Separating who a signal is from what it does lets agents reason over structure and time independently, joining the two only when a query demands it. A naïve translation of every value change would simply move the scalability problem from the filesystem into the database. BTTF instead applies coverage-aware pruning during on-the-fly database generation: • Clock pruning . High-frequency clock toggles dominate table size while carrying little debug information; since every row in signal_changes is timestamped, clock transitions can be skipped at insertion time without losing temporal anchoring. • On-the-fly inactive-signal pruning ( zero / avg ). To cope with duplicate VCD identifiers and inactive nets, the ingestion engine maintains a lightweight hash map ( vcd_id_to_db_id ) alongside a per-signal transition counter ( signal_change_count ). This bookkeeping enables two graduated policies: dropping statically silent zero-toggle wires ( zero ), or additionally dropping nets whose toggle rate falls below the design-wide average ( avg ). • Batched insertion. Row-by-row insertion incurs severe SQLite transaction overhead. Grouping transitions into batched writes removes this bottleneck at ingestion time. 3.2 LLM-Driven Agent Orchestration On top of the generated waves.db , BTTF conducts verification through a collaborative multi-agent architecture. The main Orchestration Agent decomposes a natural-language query into sub-goals, routes them to specialized agents with own toolsets, and audits the merged answer. • Analysis Agent. Armed with schema-aware multi-query execution tools, it composes SQLite queries over the two tables to handle scope discovery, event inspection, and toggle counting. For complex tasks such as power hotspot detection, it leverages an iterative function-calling loop to execute multi-turn queries and aggregate multi-cycle signal statistics. • Verification Agent. Tying waveform anomalies back to version-controlled source by evaluating SVA rules ( ASSERT , ASSERT_STATIC , ASSERT_NEVER , ASSERT_KNOWN , COVER ) through the regular expression (REGEX) assignment. • Evaluation Agent. Before any root-cause analysis is returned, this agent audits candidate queries against five criteria: (1) correctness —filtering, aggregation, and join fidelity to user intent; (2) completeness —inclusion of all required columns and time conditions; (3) efficiency —proper indexing and avoidance of redundant joins; (4) schema adherence —strict conformance to the two-table schema; and (5) context understanding —correct inference of implicit simulation timescales and hierarchy scopes. Under the orchestrator, agents communicate solely through a dynamic session context maintained across turns; together with a self-correction loop on failed queries, this shared-memory discipline lets each agent stay narrowly specialized without losing global coherence. Furthermore, when an assertion rule is violated even after self-correction, the agent autonomously isolates the exact violation timestamp and pinpoints the problematic sub-signals responsible for the failure (see Appendix A.1 for detailed root-cause diagnostics). 4 Results Experimental setup. items.content: Computer Science > Artificial Intelligence arXiv:2610.06765 (cs) [Submitted on 5 Oct 2026] Title: Conditional Rank Allocation for Taxonomy-Aware Medical Language Model Adaptation Authors: Guangyuan Dong , Ziwei Hong , Xuehao Zhou , Zidong Yu , Bingchen Liu , Kehan Liu , Chuang Liu , Rong Fu , Yuchao Hou View a PDF of the paper titled Conditional Rank Allocation for Taxonomy-Aware Medical Language Model Adaptation, by Guangyuan Dong and 8 other authors View PDF HTML (experimental) Abstract: Medical question answering spans specialties and clinical operations that may benefit from different adaptation directions. We propose ARBOR, a parameter-efficient method that selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis for each question. An additive gate combines question representations, specialty tags, operation tags, and their interaction; a learned coefficient scales the adapter residual. An illustrative separation under orthogonal, equiprobable subtasks shows how conditional selection can avoid an approximation floor faced by a fixed update with the same active rank. This result motivates the design without asserting a corresponding bound for medical corpora. On Qwen3-8B across CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA, five-seed experiments yield 69.69% mean accuracy across benchmarks, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points, respectively. The reported advantage over LoRA r16 increases from 0.08 to 1.94 points as training expands from one to seven specialties. Tag perturbations and atom masking support the usefulness of clinical routing, while atom clusters align with the supplied specialty labels (adjusted Rand index 0.62). Calibration, transfer, and measured costs further characterize the method. These findings support structured conditional adaptation for medical QA, while leaving clinical safety and broader deployment untested. items.content: Conditional Rank Allocation for Taxonomy-Aware Medical Language Model Adaptation Guangyuan Dong 1,†,‡ , Ziwei Hong 4,† , Xuehao Zhou 2,3,† , Zidong Yu 6 , Bingchen Liu 5,† Kehan Liu 1 , Chuang Liu, Rong Fu, Yuchao Hou * Affiliation: 1 National University of Singapore, Singapore 2 Department of Urology, Shanghai General Hospital, Shanghai, China 3 Shanghai Jiao Tong University School of Medicine, Shanghai, China 4 University of Pennsylvania, USA 5 Shandong University, China 6 Syracuse University, USA Email: guangyuan@u.nus.edu † These authors contributed equally. ‡ Project Lead. * Corresponding author. Abstract Medical question answering spans specialties and clinical operations that may benefit from different adaptation directions. We propose Arbor , a parameter-efficient method that selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis for each question. An additive gate combines question representations, specialty tags, operation tags, and their interaction; a learned coefficient scales the adapter residual. An illustrative separation under orthogonal, equiprobable subtasks shows how conditional selection can avoid an approximation floor faced by a fixed update with the same active rank. This result motivates the design without asserting a corresponding bound for medical corpora. On Qwen3-8B across CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA, five-seed experiments yield 69.69% mean accuracy across benchmarks, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points, respectively. The reported advantage over LoRA r16 increases from 0.08 to 1.94 points as training expands from one to seven specialties. Tag perturbations and atom masking support the usefulness of clinical routing, while atom clusters align with the supplied specialty labels (adjusted Rand index 0.62). Calibration, transfer, and measured costs further characterize the method. These findings support structured conditional adaptation for medical QA, while leaving clinical safety and broader deployment untested. Index Terms: parameter-efficient fine-tuning, conditional rank allocation, medical question answering, clinical taxonomy I Introduction Medical question answering spans specialties and clinical operations that may benefit from different adaptation directions. Standard LoRA applies one low-rank update to every input [ 1 ] ; a drug-interaction question and an anatomy fact therefore share the same adaptation subspace. Conditional selection offers a way to specialize updates while reusing a stored basis. Specialty and clinical operation describe complementary aspects of a question. A specialty identifies its knowledge context, while an operation describes the requested task, such as recall, diagnosis, or treatment. Questions within one specialty can require different operations, and the same operation can recur across specialties. This motivates separate routing contributions together with a pair-specific interaction, rather than a single undifferentiated clinical label. Arbor (Adaptive Rank allocation with Budgeted On-demand Routing) selects rank-one atoms per question using an additive gate over question representations, specialty, operation, and their interaction. A learned coefficient scales the residual, and a discrete mask records active components. Our contribution is this clinical structure and its evaluation, building on existing rank-level routing rather than introducing that mechanism. An orthogonal-subtask construction illustrates a representational advantage at matched active rank. Its assumptions do not imply monotonic gains for real medical corpora or explain comparisons against rank-16 LoRA when only seven specialties are tested. We examine these gains empirically through heterogeneity, tag perturbations, and atom masking. Across four Chinese and English benchmarks and five seeds, Arbor reaches 69.69% mean accuracy, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points. Clustering evaluates alignment with supplied clinical labels; calibration, transfer, and measured costs characterize the method beyond accuracy. Active rank, parameter count, and runtime are distinguished throughout. Fig. 1: Arbor overview. Clinical priors and frozen question features feed four additive routing branches. Straight-through top- κ \kappa selection activates four of sixteen stored rank-one atoms; a learned coefficient scales their contribution alongside the frozen backbone. Mask and scale are shared across target layers. The training objective and question-level routing record are shown below. Highlighted mask positions are schematic. II Related Work and Positioning LoRA uses a shared low-rank update [ 1 ] , while AdaLoRA reallocates rank across modules [ 2 ] . MoELoRA routes among adapters [ 3 ] ; HydraLoRA shares a down-projection while diversifying expert up-projections [ 4 ] . Biomedical post-training also includes BFT, which reweights token- and sample-level losses for knowledge alignment [ 5 ] . Knowledge-guided pathway prototypes in scProtoTransformer provide interpretable biological representations [ 6 ] . Input-conditioned reuse of learned primitives also appears in PriMD [ 7 ] , which retrieves semantic primitives to compensate for missing modalities. Arbor applies conditional selection to rank-one parameter updates for medical question answering. Arrow [ 8 ] , MeteoRA [ 9 ] , and LoRA-Mixer [ 10 ] compose pretrained adapter pools; MedAdapter [ 11 ] verifies candidate answers at test time. These pipelines differ from adapters trained under our common CMB-source budget. Matching active rank, stored rank, or parameter count guarantees neither equal runtime nor identical capacity. In biomedical named entity recognition, MITE combines code-formatted instruction tuning with entity-level voting [ 12 ] , while GAMA combines verified annotation guidelines with schema-constrained generation [ 13 ] . Arbor uses clinical tags to condition parameter updates for question answering. SMoRA treats individual ranks as experts with straight-through selection [ 14 ] . Arbor adds specialty, operation, and interaction logits plus residual scaling, and evaluates their contribution to clinical routing and supplied-label alignment. III Why Conditional Rank Allocation Helps We give an illustrative linear separation, not a medical-model risk bound. Let Δ j = B : , j A j , : \Delta_{j}=B_{:,j}A_{j,:} , j ∈ [ R ] j\in[R] . Fixed selection applies Δ S = ∑ j ∈ S Δ j \Delta_{S}=\sum_{j\in S}\Delta_{j} to every h ⁡ ( x ) h(x) ; conditional selection applies Δ S ⁡ ( x ) ​ h ​ ( x ) \Delta_{S(x)}h(x) with | S ⁡ ( x ) | = κ |S(x)|=\kappa . Constant routing includes fixed supports. Strict inclusion requires nondegenerate atoms and inputs enabling outputs unavailable to constant routing; it need not hold for every basis. Scope of the argument Orthogonality, equiprobable regions, and correct routing are assumed. Overlap, imbalance, routing errors, and nonlinear representations alter the comparison. More medical specialties need not mean more independent target directions. Rank-16 LoRA has zero floor in Eq. ( 2 ) for m ≤ 7 m\leq 7 , so its heterogeneity comparison is empirical, not bound validation. Matched rank-4 sweeps and multiple specialty combinations would strengthen the connection. A generalization analysis must also account for input-dependent router complexity, not only support counts. IV-B Clinically structured gate Question representation h x h_{x} is the mean-pooled frozen-backbone hidden state over question and option tokens at layer ⌊ L / 2 ⌋ \lfloor L/2\rfloor . The gate combines semantic and clinical logits: a ⁡ ( x ) = a h ​ ( h x ) + a s ​ ( s ⁡ ( x ) ) + a o ​ ( o ⁡ ( x ) ) + a s ​ o ​ ( s ⁡ ( x ) , o ⁡ ( x ) ) . a(x)=a_{h}(h_{x})+a_{s}(s(x))+a_{o}(o(x))+a_{so}(s(x),o(x)). (4) Here a h a_{h} is a two-layer MLP; a s , a o , a s ​ o a_{s},a_{o},a_{so} are embedding tables for specialty, operation, and their pair. This additive form allows each clinical axis to contribute separately while retaining pair-specific effects. We compute p ⁡ ( x ) \displaystyle p(x) = softmax ⁡ ( a ⁡ ( x ) / τ ) , ζ ⁡ ( x ) = ST ​ - ​ top ​ - ​ κ ​ ( p ⁡ ( x ) ) , \displaystyle=\mathrm{softmax}(a(x)/\tau),\quad\zeta(x)=\mathrm{ST\text{-}top\text{-}\kappa}(p(x)), (5) ρ ⁡ ( x ) \displaystyle\rho(x) = σ ⁡ ( w ρ ⊤ ​ h x + b ρ ) . \displaystyle=\sigma(w_{\rho}^{\top}h_{x}+b_{\rho}). (6) The forward pass selects the κ \kappa largest entries with a binary mask; a straight-through estimator passes gradients through soft probabilities [ 16 , 17 ] . The coefficient ρ \rho learns how strongly to inject the residual. It is neither calibrated uncertainty nor a validated measure of clinical safety. Gate features must be obtained from the frozen backbone before the conditioned adapter pass; their extraction or caching is part of the implementation cost. IV-C Clinical tags Seven specialty labels and eight operation labels come from available metadata or deterministic rules on the question and options. For example, specialty rules include drug/dose/contraindication for Pharmacy, nursing/care plan for Nursing, and incidence/screening/vaccine for Public Health; the fallback is Clinical Medicine. Operation rules cover diagnosis, treatment, medication, examination, mechanism, nursing action, and prevention, with Recall as fallback. Gold answers are excluded, and target-benchmark labels are not used to tune rules or routing. Two annotators labeled a 500-item sample (Table I ); specialty and operation tags achieve 91.4% and 84.6% accuracy, respectively. Inter-annotator agreement is κ = 0.86 \kappa=0.86 and 0.79 0.79 ; rule coverage is 100% through the fallback labels. These measurements describe the sampled items and do not establish equal tag quality across languages or datasets. TABLE I: Clinical-prior validation on 500 annotated questions. Agreement is inter-annotator κ \kappa . Axis Accuracy Coverage Majority Agreement Specialty (7) 91.4% 100% 28.6% 0.86 Operation (8) 84.6% 100% 24.2% 0.79 IV-D Training and computation Answer-only supervised fine-tuning uses ℒ = ℒ ans + λ ent ​ ℒ ent + λ bal ​ ℒ bal + λ orth ​ ℒ orth + λ axis ​ ℒ axis . \begin{split}\mathcal{L}=\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ans}}&+\lambda_{\mathrm{ent}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{ent}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{bal}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{bal}}\\ &+\lambda_{\mathrm{orth}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{orth}}+\lambda_{\mathrm{axis}}\mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{axis}}.\end{split} (7) Entropy and balancing terms regularize routing; ℒ orth = ‖ A ​ A ⊤ ⊙ ( 1 − I ) ‖ F 2 \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{orth}}=\|AA^{\top}\odot(1-I)\|_{F}^{2} penalizes correlation between atom directions. Decorrelation also regularizes molecular interaction features in DSIL-DDI [ 18 ] . A supervised contrastive ℒ axis \mathcal{L}_{\mathrm{axis}} encourages questions from the same specialty to have similar routing distributions. Since specialty labels enter both the gate and this objective, clustering evaluates alignment with supplied labels rather than independent discovery of a taxonomy. We use R = 16 R=16 , κ = 4 \kappa=4 , α = 32 \alpha=32 , τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 , and regularizer weights ( 0.01 , 0.001 , 0.1 , 0.5 ) (0.01,0.001,0.1,0.5) in the order above; remaining training settings are in Section V . Rank selection costs O ⁡ ( R ​ log ⁡ κ ) O(R\log\kappa) once per question. Activating four atoms does not imply the parameter count or runtime of rank-4 LoRA: the full basis is stored, and routing, feature extraction, and the adapter implementation contribute to measured cost. V Experimental Setup Data and evaluation Using Qwen3-8B [ 19 ] , source training uses a route-balanced CMB [ 20 ] subset of 4,200 questions (600 per specialty), disjoint from evaluation. Main evaluation uses Chinese CMB (4,149 questions) and CMExam [ 21 ] , and English MedQA [ 22 ] (700 test questions) and MedMCQA [ 23 ] (700 validation questions). PubMedQA [ 24 ] provides out-of-family evaluation. Accuracy is primary; macro is the unweighted four-benchmark average, not pooled question accuracy. Exact evaluation manifests and the CMExam split and sample count remain reproducibility limitations. Training and statistical analysis Trainable methods use 400 updates, effective batch size 8, learning rate 10 − 4 10^{-4} , maximum sequence length 768, answer-only supervised fine-tuning, greedy decoding, and a common answer parser and prompt template within each language. Arbor uses R = 16 R=16 , κ = 4 \kappa=4 , α = 32 \alpha=32 , τ = 0.5 \tau=0.5 , and ( λ ent , λ bal , λ orth , λ axis ) = ( 0.01 , 0.001 , 0.1 , 0.5 ) (\lambda_{\rm ent},\lambda_{\rm bal},\lambda_{\rm orth},\lambda_{\rm axis})=(0.01,0.001,0.1,0.5) , targeting the q/k/v/o/gate/up/down projections. Hyperparameters were selected using a 400-question held-out source slice, without target-benchmark labels. Runs use an A100-80GB, PyTorch 2.3, and bf16. Results are means and standard deviations over seeds { 13 , 29 , 47 , 71 , 97 } \{13,29,47,71,97\} . The paired differences and their 95% confidence intervals in Fig. 2 summarize variation across training seeds; they do not quantify uncertainty from resampling the benchmark population. Comparators LoRA r4 matches the active rank, LoRA r16 the atom-bank size, and LoRA r24 approximately the trainable parameter count. We also compare DoRA [ 25 ] r24, HydraLoRA (four heads), and MoELoRA (four rank-8 experts, top-2). The rank-wise control uses an r16/top-4 adapter inspired by SMoRA [ 14 ] , but removes clinical branches, their interaction, axis contrast, orthogonality, and injection scaling. It therefore compares the complete design with a simplified router and does not isolate the effect of clinical tags alone. Adapter-library results are reported separately because they compose pretrained adapters and are not matched source-training comparisons. TABLE II: Qwen3-8B medical QA accuracy (%). Abstract Medical question answering spans specialties and clinical operations that may benefit from different adaptation directions. We propose Arbor , a parameter-efficient method that selects rank-one components from a shared low-rank basis for each question. An additive gate combines question representations, specialty tags, operation tags, and their interaction; a learned coefficient scales the adapter residual. An illustrative separation under orthogonal, equiprobable subtasks shows how conditional selection can avoid an approximation floor faced by a fixed update with the same active rank. This result motivates the design without asserting a corresponding bound for medical corpora. On Qwen3-8B across CMB, CMExam, MedQA, and MedMCQA, five-seed experiments yield 69.69% mean accuracy across benchmarks, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points, respectively. The reported advantage over LoRA r16 increases from 0.08 to 1.94 points as training expands from one to seven specialties. Tag perturbations and atom masking support the usefulness of clinical routing, while atom clusters align with the supplied specialty labels (adjusted Rand index 0.62). Calibration, transfer, and measured costs further characterize the method. These findings support structured conditional adaptation for medical QA, while leaving clinical safety and broader deployment untested. Index Terms: parameter-efficient fine-tuning, conditional rank allocation, medical question answering, clinical taxonomy I Introduction Medical question answering spans specialties and clinical operations that may benefit from different adaptation directions. Standard LoRA applies one low-rank update to every input [ 1 ] ; a drug-interaction question and an anatomy fact therefore share the same adaptation subspace. Conditional selection offers a way to specialize updates while reusing a stored basis. Specialty and clinical operation describe complementary aspects of a question. A specialty identifies its knowledge context, while an operation describes the requested task, such as recall, diagnosis, or treatment. Questions within one specialty can require different operations, and the same operation can recur across specialties. This motivates separate routing contributions together with a pair-specific interaction, rather than a single undifferentiated clinical label. Arbor (Adaptive Rank allocation with Budgeted On-demand Routing) selects rank-one atoms per question using an additive gate over question representations, specialty, operation, and their interaction. A learned coefficient scales the residual, and a discrete mask records active components. Our contribution is this clinical structure and its evaluation, building on existing rank-level routing rather than introducing that mechanism. An orthogonal-subtask construction illustrates a representational advantage at matched active rank. Its assumptions do not imply monotonic gains for real medical corpora or explain comparisons against rank-16 LoRA when only seven specialties are tested. We examine these gains empirically through heterogeneity, tag perturbations, and atom masking. Across four Chinese and English benchmarks and five seeds, Arbor reaches 69.69% mean accuracy, exceeding LoRA r16 and MoELoRA by 1.26 and 1.30 percentage points. Clustering evaluates alignment with supplied clinical labels; calibration, transfer, and measured costs characterize the method beyond accuracy. Active rank, parameter count, and runtime are distinguished throughout. Fig. 1: Arbor overview. Clinical priors and frozen question features feed four additive routing branches. Straight-through top- κ \kappa selection activates four of sixteen stored rank-one atoms; a learned coefficient scales their contribution alongside the frozen backbone. Mask and scale are shared across target layers. The training objective and question-level routing record are shown below. Highlighted mask positions are schematic. II Related Work and Positioning LoRA uses a shared low-rank update [ 1 ] , while AdaLoRA reallocates rank across modules [ 2 ] . MoELoRA routes among adapters [ 3 ] ; HydraLoRA shares a down-projection while diversifying expert up-projections [ 4 ] . Biomedical post-training also includes BFT, which reweights token- and sample-level losses for knowledge alignment [ 5 ] . Knowledge-guided pathway prototypes in scProtoTransformer provide interpretable biological representations [ 6 ] . Input-conditioned reuse of learned primitives also appears in PriMD [ 7 ] , which retrieves semantic primitives to compensate for missing modalities. Arbor applies conditional selection to rank-one parameter updates for medical question answering. Arrow [ 8 ] , MeteoRA [ 9 ] , and LoRA-Mixer [ 10 ] compose pretrained adapter pools; MedAdapter [ 11 ] verifies candidate answers at test time. These pipelines differ from adapters trained under our common CMB-source budget. Matching active rank, stored rank, or parameter count guarantees neither equal runtime nor identical capacity. In biomedical named entity recognition, MITE combines code-formatted instruction tuning with entity-level voting [ 12 ] , while GAMA combines verified annotation guidelines with schema-constrained generation [ 13 ] . Arbor uses clinical tags to condition parameter updates for question answering. SMoRA treats individual ranks as experts with straight-through selection [ 14 ] . Arbor adds specialty, operation, and interaction logits plus residual scaling, and evaluates their contribution to clinical routing and supplied-label alignment. items.content: At a glance End-to-end forecasting: A machine learning pipeline uses forecast-time solar-wind information to generate location-specific risk estimates for 66,935 substations in the continental United States. Physics and place: The system combines Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) forecasts with local latitude, geology, and ground conductivity. Advance warning: The pipeline detected nearly 80% of major space-weather events during the evaluation period and can warn grid operators 30 to 60 minutes before a specific risk appears. Forecasting a threat to critical infrastructure During the May 2024 geomagnetic storm, utilities across North America prepared for possible impacts as auroras extended far beyond their usual range. The storm would degrade GPS accuracy and satellite operations, impacting farm operations in North America and Europe. Modern society depends on reliable electric power, yet extreme space-weather events can induce currents in transmission networks that damage equipment and increase operational risk. The challenge is not only knowing that a storm is approaching, but estimating when and where its effects could be most severe with enough warning for grid operators to respond. During my summer internship at Microsoft Research, I developed a machine learning system that forecasts space-weather risk across 66,935 substations in the continental United States. The system measures how the sun’s activity can affect the earth’s magnetic field and, ultimately, the power grid. It combines solar-wind observations, forecasts of the Auroral Electrojet (AE) and Disturbance Storm Time (Dst) indices, physics-informed constraints, local geological conductivity, and grid-infrastructure data to produce location-specific risk estimates 30-60 minutes ahead of potential impact. Building an end-to-end prediction pipeline Space-weather prediction is difficult because it spans several coupled systems. The solar wind changes rapidly, its interaction with Earth’s magnetosphere is irregular, and the resulting ground effects depend on local conditions. Regions with resistive bedrock can experience stronger geomagnetically induced currents (GICs) than regions with more conductive geology. Transmission-line orientation, latitude, and other power-system characteristics further influence the exposure of individual assets. video series On Second Thought A video series with Sinead Bovell built around the questions everyone’s asking about AI. With expert voices from across Microsoft, we break down the tension and promise of this rapidly changing technology, exploring what’s evolving and what’s possible. Explore the series Opens in a new tab The pipeline addresses this complexity in three stages, shown in Figure 1. First, solar-wind measurements from the L1 Lagrange point are used to generate forecasts of the AE and Dst indices, while geological conductivity and location features are assembled for each substation. Second, a gradient-boosting model combines these forecasted and location-specific inputs to estimate dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC risk. Finally, the resulting predictions are converted into location-specific risk estimates and aggregated into a continental risk assessment. A system of 50 AI agents helped explore features, validation strategies, and model configurations across the pipeline. Only public data sources were used, included NASA OMNI and NASA-aggregated Kyoto World Data Center data, INTERMAGNET and U.S. Geological Survey magnetometer observations, and GridSFM-derived grid data. Figure 1. End-to-end forecasting pipeline from L1 solar-wind measurements to location-specific risk estimates across 66,935 U.S. substations. Evaluating geomagnetic forecasts and infrastructure risk The AE predictor was designed to forecast rare, high-intensity geomagnetic activity that drives infrastructure risk. In the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the model produced forecasts spanning nearly the full observed range of AE activity and outperformed several empirical solar-wind-based approaches. The Dst predictor provided an additional signal describing large-scale geomagnetic storm strength. During the most geomagnetically active periods of the 2020-2026 evaluation period, the machine-learning model outperformed the Burton equation on 62.2% of individual hours. The model also produced a substantially wider prediction range than Burton-style approaches and improved severe-event detection in the end-to-end forecasting system by 1.2 percentage points when combined with AE forecasts. Predictor Result Baseline comparison Impact AE 410.2 nT RMSE Lower RMSE than empirical and solar-wind-only baselines Captures extreme-event activity used by the GIC forecasting system Dst 7.2 nT RMSE Outperformed Burton on 62.2% of peak-activity hours and provided wider prediction range +1.2pp severe storm detection when integrated into final GIC system The GIC risk stage was evaluated differently. There is no equivalent widely deployed operational system that provides a direct industry benchmark for this calculation, so the machine learning model was compared with simple linear regression. As Figure 2 shows, the system achieved detection rates of 76.5% for major events (≥10 nT/min), 81.2% for severe events (≥20 nT/min), and 64.1% for extreme events (≥50 nT/min). False-alarm rates increased with storm severity, reflecting the trade-off between missed events and cautious alerts. Performance varied by latitude, with the highest detection rates at northern stations where geomagnetic activity is strongest. Figure 2. Detection rates across storm-severity thresholds for regionally different substations, with a comparison between the average POD for each severity tier. Translating predictions into continental risk assessments The final stage translates predicted geomagnetic activity into location-specific estimates of dB/dt, the rate of magnetic-field change associated with GIC exposure. Rather than issuing a single alert for the continental United States, the system combines storm conditions with each substation’s latitude and geological factor. This produces continuous risk estimates that can distinguish lower-risk locations from areas where resistive geology can amplify ground-level effects. Figure 3 illustrates the output for a representative major-storm scenario. The map is a demonstration of the model’s continental-scale output, not a record of a live operational event. It shows how a grid operator or planner could move from a broad space-weather warning toward a more targeted view of which locations may warrant closer analysis. The current pipeline produced estimates for all 66,935 substations in approximately 333 milliseconds during measured inference, allowing many scenarios to be evaluated quickly. Figure 3. Demonstration of a continental GIC risk assessment under a representative major-storm scenario. Colors indicate modeled risk levels across 66,935 substations. Implications and looking forward This work demonstrates how physics-grounded machine learning could support more specific and timely assessment of space-weather exposure. Earlier, location-specific information could help utilities prioritize engineering review and consider targeted protective actions, such as adjusting reactive-power reserves or temporarily reconfiguring parts of the network. Further validation with utilities and operational data would be needed before the system could be used in grid operations. The project also connects with broader Microsoft Research work on AI for power systems. The open grid-data pipeline provided realistic U.S. transmission models, while GridSFM applies deep learning to AC optimal power flow for fast scenario analysis. Together, these efforts point toward richer planning and resilience workflows that combine hazard forecasts, grid topology, and power-flow analysis. Extend forecast horizons: Explore temporal-transformer approaches that capture longer-range patterns in solar-wind data and move beyond the current 30-60-minute window. Scale internationally: Adapt the system to additional regions while accounting for different geological conditions and grid topologies. Integrate with grid operations: Evaluate how forecasts could support existing decision-making and engineering-review workflows before considering higher levels of automation. Provide transformer-level risk: Add asset-specific characteristics to move from substation-level estimates toward more granular assessments of critical equipment. Related Microsoft Research work Video playback requires cookie consent GridSFM: A new, small foundation model for the electric grid Building realistic electric transmission grid dataset at scale: a pipeline from open dataset Acknowledgements Special thanks to my mentors Weiwei Yang and Spencer Fowers for their guidance throughout this project, and to Amber Hoak , Weishung Liu , and Andrea Britto for their editorial and technical feedback. Financial paper that is insured by the FDIC's Temporary Liquidity Guarantee Program is not excluded from relevant indexes, nor is any financial or nonfinancial commercial paper that may be directly or indirectly affected by one or more of the Federal Reserve's liquidity facilities. Thus the rates published after September 19, 2008, likely reflect the direct or indirect effects of the new temporary programs and, accordingly, likely are not comparable for some purposes to rates published prior to that period. 7. The rate charged for discounts made and advances extended under the Federal Reserve's primary credit discount window program, which became effective January 9, 2003. This rate replaces that for adjustment credit, which was discontinued after January 8, 2003. For further information, see www.federalreserve.gov/boarddocs/press/bcreg/2002/200210312/default.htm . The rate reported is that for the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. Historical series for the rate on adjustment credit as well as the rate on primary credit are available at www.federalreserve.gov/releases/h15/data.htm . 9. Yields on actively traded non-inflation-indexed issues adjusted to constant maturities. The 30-year Treasury constant maturity series was discontinued on February 18, 2002, and reintroduced on February 9, 2006. From February 18, 2002, to February 9, 2006, the U.S. Treasury published a factor for adjusting the daily nominal 20-year constant maturity in order to estimate a 30-year nominal rate. The historical adjustment factor can be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . Source: U.S. Treasury. 10. Yields on Treasury inflation protected securities (TIPS) adjusted to constant maturities. Source: U.S. Treasury. Additional information on both nominal and inflation-indexed yields may be found at home.treasury.gov/policy-issues/financing-the-government/interest-rate-statistics . 11. Based on the unweighted average bid yields for all TIPS with remaining terms to maturity of more than 10 years. Note: Current and historical H.15 data, along with weekly, monthly, and annual averages, are available on the Board's Data Download Program (DDP) at www.federalreserve.gov/datadownload/Choose.aspx?rel=H15 ). Weekly, monthly and annual rates are averages of business days unless otherwise noted. Description of the Treasury Nominal and Inflation-Indexed Constant Maturity Series Yields on Treasury nominal securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated by the U.S. Treasury from the daily yield curve for non-inflation-indexed Treasury securities. This curve, which relates the yield on a security to its time to maturity, is based on the closing market bid yields on actively traded Treasury securities in the over-the-counter market. These market yields are calculated from composites of quotations obtained by the Federal Reserve Bank of New York. The constant maturity yield values are read from the yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 1, 3, and 6 months and 1, 2, 3, 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. This method provides a yield for a 10-year maturity, for example, even if no outstanding security has exactly 10 years remaining to maturity. Similarly, yields on inflation-indexed securities at “constant maturity” are interpolated from the daily yield curve for Treasury inflation protected securities in the over-the-counter market. The inflation-indexed constant maturity yields are read from this yield curve at fixed maturities, currently 5, 7, 10, 20, and 30 years. Back to Top Last Update: October 05, 2026 Back to Top
